subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

speechtext:
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 18, to readjust the representation in the House of Commons.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is to provide for redistribution under the provisions of the British North America Act as amended1 in

1946. The bill itself is in the form in which it has been since 1903, but is not identical with previous bills owing to the fact that the number of constituencies is now fixed at 255 and not subject to change as heretofore. As in the past it is intended to set up a special committee of the house composed of members of all parties to consider and recommend the boundaries of the constituencies to be adopted. When the bill has received second reading it will be referred to this committee with the schedule in blank. When the recommendations of the committee have been approved by the house, it will be incorporated in the schedule as a part of this bill.
It is my intention to ask my colleague, the Secretary of State, to take charge of the bill on second reading.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: In view of the large accumulation of questions on the order paper, I should like to ask the Prime Minister if the government will give favourable consideration to having these questions answered at an early day, say tomorrow or perhaps Monday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS ON TIIE ORDER PAPER
speechtext: It might be arranged to have the questions answered on Monday. I should like to take advantage of the moment to say to my hon. friend that no question has been raised by the government thus far in regard to the many questions which have been asked on the orders of the day, for the reason that we have recognized that questions were not being answered from time to time during the week as they ordinarily would be. But I think I should direct the attention of the house, as I did last year, to the fact that a great deal of time is taken up in the asking of questions requiring oral answers, when the questions should be placed on the order paper and answered in the regular way. I hope the house will feel that it is in the interests of all hon. members that the number of questions asked on the orders of the day should be limited as much as possible.

speechtext: May I aSk the Prime Minister if notices of motion for the production of papers as well as questions might come before the house at the time he has indicated?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS ON TIIE ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
I see no reason why that should not be done.

Inquiries of the Ministry____

subtopic: ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS ON TIIE ORDER PAPER
speechtext: With regards to questions on the orders of the day, may I ask the Prime Minister if he will adopt a different attitude from that which has been adopted in the past? In the British House of Commons, as the Prime Minister knows, the first hour is given to the answering of questions orally and in writing. In one hour during which I watched the British house in operation eighty-two questions were answered, as well as supplementary questions arising from time to time. In this house we have gone to the opposite extreme. As a matter of fact I think the only criticism of this house is that we do not ask the government enough questions. The government get off far too easily in matters of this kind. I should not like the Prime Minister's words to be regarded as indicative of the policy which will be pursued from now on, because it is in the interests of the country that these questions be asked freely and that plenty of latitude be given. After all, that is how the people find out about the business of the country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ANSWERING OF QUESTIONS ON TIIE ORDER PAPER
speechtext: May I say to my hon. friend the government is not objecting in any way to any number of questions. The point is as to the time at which and the manner in which questions should be asked and answered. Like my hon. friend, I have been in the British house and have followed its proceedings. My recollection of the questions being asked there is that all appear on the order paper and are answered by the ministers from the order paper, much as we do here. There is no limit to the number that may be asked, provided that they conform to the rules. It happens that in London there are likely to be very many more subjects touched upon during a question hour than there would be here. I would point out that the questions which are asked orally and which are expected to be answered orally are those which are asked as supplementary questions growing out of answers made to questions which are already on the order paper. They are not new subjects; that is the point I wish to make. The ministers are not expected to answer questions of which notice has not been given and which do not appear on the order paper, unless, as I have stated, they are questions arising from questions on the order paper or dealing with some matter of great urgency of which prior notice has been given to Mr. Speaker. Again may I say there is no desire to limit the number of questions but simply to have the questions asked and answered in a manner which will ensure accuracy and which will help expedite the business of the house.

maintopic: THREATENED STRIKE OF COAL MINERS IN NOVA SCOTIA-REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: THREATENED STRIKE OF COAL MINERS IN NOVA SCOTIA-REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like at this time to make a report to the house on
Inquiries oj the Ministry

negotiations with respect to the threatened strike of the coal miners of Nova Scotia.
On Friday night, January 31, the miners, about 13,000 in number, belonging to district 26 of the United Mine Workers of America, went on strike, closing down operations of the Dominion Steel and Coal Company, Acadia Coal Company Limited, Old Sydney Collieries Limited and The Cumberland Railway and Coal Company. The miners returned to work for the night shift on Monday, February 3. The strike was called off in view of the appointment of Mr. Justice W. F. Carroll of the supreme court of Nova Scotia as a commissioner to look into the merits of the dispute between the men and the companies. The arrangement was that the men would remain at work until February 15 in order to give Mr. Justice Carroll time to make his investigation and report to myself as Minister of Labour.
Mr. Justice Carroll's report was received on Tuesday, February 11, and I now table a copy for the information of the house. It contains recommendations as follows:
(1) That an increase of $1.40 per day should be paid effective from and after February 1, 1947, of which $1 per day would be provided by an agreement based on production as proposed by the companies and the remaining 40 cents by other means.
2.	That a welfare fund be created1 by paying into a special account three cents per ton on the coal produced, the same arrangement put into effect in regard to the western Canada coal miners.
3.	That a request for the -inception of a pension fund be deferred until there could be an actuarial check and conferences with the government of Nova Scotia.
I table also copies of:
1.	Telegram sent to Mr. Justice Carroll dated February 12.
2.	Telegram received from Mr. Freeman Jenkins, president, district 26. United Mine Workers of America, dated February 13.
3.	Telegram received from the Nova Scotia government, dated February 13.

maintopic: THREATENED STRIKE OF COAL MINERS IN NOVA SCOTIA-REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether the recommendations of Mr. Justice Carroll have been reviewed by the workmen and the operators in the maritime provinces, and if so, whether they were found acceptable? If not, when shall we get a report on whether or not the recommendations of the commissioner will be complied with?

maintopic: THREATENED STRIKE OF COAL MINERS IN NOVA SCOTIA-REPORT ON NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, I did this deliberately. As soon as copies of the report were in the hands of the parties con-
cerned I thought it well that a copy should be placed on the table of this house. I have no knowledge of the attitude of either the mine workers or the employers in regard to that report, but my hon. friend may rest assured that no stone will be left unturned by the dominion Department of Labour to prevent a walk-out on February 15.
On the orders of the day:

Yesterday the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked a question in reference to labour relations. At that time I read a telegram that had been dispatched to the respective provincial governments.
In my wire of January 28, I proposed repealing schedule A to P.C. 1003 on March 31 next "which would have the effect of bringing jurisdiction in the matter of labour relations back to a peacetime position. All replies received agreed to this proposal. Certain provinces, namely, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia adopted the dominion regulations and1 made them applicable to provincial industries, and in my wire I asked the provinces if it would be any advantage to them to continue the existing arrangement, including joint administration, until May 15, 1947, subject to the provinces having the option of discontinuing the arrangement at an earlier date if they so desired; and replies indicate the provinces desire this be done.
All provinces have formally replied to my telegram of January 28 except the province of Manitoba, and verbal advice has been received from the minister of labour for that province to the effect that he intended to recommend to his government that it request the extension until May 15, 1947.

The minister spoke about coal mines in Nova Scotia. I believe the coal mines at Minto, New Brunswick, are under district number 26. Do Mr. Justice Carroll's recommendations apply to those mines and miners, the same as in Nova Scotia?

The president of district 26 negotiates with both Nova Scotia and New Brunswick collieries. I would assume that under those conditions whatever settlement is made will cover the whole district, which includes New Brunswick as well as Nova Scotia.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD

speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, February 12, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Claxton-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair:
That it is expedient to amend the Department of National Defence Act to provide for the appointment of not more than three associate deputy ministers of national defence and to give the governor in council power, by regulation, to administer the service estates of members of the forces who die on active service or while receiving hospital treatment or institutional care under the Department of Veterans Affairs on account of any disability suffered or incurred during their service as such members; to provide for the establishment of a defence research board charged with the duties of conducting and coordinating research and development tor defence and of establishing scholarships and making grants in aid; and to provide further for salaries, remuneration and expenses of the board and of a pension or superannuation fund tor the benefit of employees out of moneys appropriated by parliament.
Mr, PEARKES: A sentence in this resolution refers to the administration of service estates of members of the forces who die on active service or while receiving hospital treatment or institutional care under the Department of Veterans Affairs. Would not the administration of those estates come more properly under the Department of Veterans Affairs, or some department of government other than National Defence, which at the present time is concerned with the training of live soldiers and with looking to the future?
-f suggest that the one minister under whom administration of the three services is now combined will have all his time fully occupied with matters of administration both in the piesent and in the future. I question the necessity of encumbering him with the estates of deceased soldiers.
for any purpose he is struck off strength. Lnder normal circumstances a soldier who is struck off strength is considered a veteran, and as such comes under the Department of

Veterans Affairs. Would it not be advisable to have the estates of soldiers who cease to be on the active list administered by the Department of Veterans Affairs? Why is it considered necessary that the minister's department should administer service estates?

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: The proposed bill will apply only to the service estates of members of the active force. The reason why the Department of Veterans Affairs is brought in is that a considerable number of soldiers are in hospitals operating under that department.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: The resolution refers to the estates of deceased soldiers, soldiers who have died^ on active service or while in institutions administered by the Department of Veterans Affairs. My contention is that the estate of any man who for any reason-death or otherwise-has ceased to be a soldier, is hardly the concern of the Department of National Defence, a department which is preparing for the future.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: While I may be anticipating the presentation of the bill, perhaps I may be permitted to say that it applies only to the estates of members of the naval, military or air forces in Canada who died during their service as such members.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
That is it; they died.
Mr. ADAMSON; The Minister of Veterans Affairs may recall a case I brought to his attention respecting a soldier who died in Christie Street hospital while under treatment, and it was the Department of Veterans Affairs which looked after it. The proposal in this measure means that the Department of National Defence will now take care of such cases. Formerly a death in a military hospital, or one operating under the Department of Veterans Affairs, was looked after by that department. Is this now to be done by the Department of National Defence?
Mr. CLAXTON; The proposed legislation makes no change in the position. Service estates are now administered under P.C. 3617, which was passed on August 27, 1946, consolidating various measures which preceded it. There is no change in the practice. The new measure will apply only to the service estates of members of the services. If at the time of their deaths they happened to be in hospitals operated by the Department of Veterans Affairs, then the same machinery will be used, but it would probably be put into effect through an officer from that department who may be on the spot, but who would be acting as an agent for the Department of National Defence.

National Defence Act

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
This measure is a big surprise to people who are interested in the welfare of members of the three branches of the armed services. I can tell you this, that while the present minister has been in his department only about two months, this is a wide departure for him to make. It starts off quite well, but I think it goes a little too far. The bar associations of this country have set up a committee to take care of the affairs of veterans, and many lawyers work for nothing to aid veterans and their estates.
It is intended to administer from Ottawa, and under three deputy ministers, the service estates of members of the forces who die on active service or while receiving hospital treatment or institutional care. A man may be up in the new Sunnybrook hospital for many reasons. A man may be on active service in one of the camps or he may be overseas. He may have a motor accident in which he is killed instantly. Why take the administration of his estate out of the hands of the local legal profession which has set up various soldier agencies and committees to handle these things? You, Mr. Chairman, were on one of those committees of the Canadian bar association which did this sort of work for nothing. It is intended to create a large department and we are going to repeat the mistake that was made between the two wars in connection with the settlement of estates, small accounts and pensions by the department.
It is intended to centralize this in the city of Ottawa when it should be spread out in the local cities and towns. This sort of work should be the duty of the municipal councils and others. The city of Toronto has a large department to handle work like this and other branches of soldiers and veterans affairs. I do not know where the government got this idea. It is going to be an expensive plan and it will not meet, the individual cases. Members of parliament will be deluged with requests for information.
There is a large department at 55 York street in Toronto. That department has done very good work no doubt. Possibly some improvements have been made, but there are still a large number of officials there. When I go there I find I have to start at the top floor and go right down to the basement. At one time there were ijbout 1,400 officials there.
When you have such a large department it will be impossible to find out what you want to find out. A veteran may die who has owned a house which he cannot get into. This man may have served in the last war and in the meantime he has spent on a house his credits and gratuity. Let us take a concrete case.
He is knocked down by a motor car. Over 102 were killed last year and nearly 10,000 were injured, many of them soldiers and soldiers' children. What are you going to do about his estate? Are you going to wait until you get the service money that is coming to him? Many of these soldiers cannot get into their own homes. This will be imposing a burden on the government which they should not have to carry. It is going to mean a large expenditure of money in research, and it certainly is not the right way to approach the question. These things should be handled close to the home of the soldier. Many of these boys are getting home after being away for a long time.
This resolution should have gone to a committee. I cannot understand the government hoping to get it passed in the twinkling of an eye. A large department is to be set up in Ottawa to handle these estates and research. That is interfering with property and civil rights and surrogate wTork which come under the jurisdiction of the provinces. This will interfere with the work being done at 55 York street, and with the work of No. 2 district. It will mean duplication and waste.
Then there is to be a defence research board established. That will be another organization as high as this building. It will just fulfil some of the duties that are being carried out elsewhere by universities and national research departments. I suppose this board will take holidays in the summer and we will not get replies to any letters that we write. The work done by the veterans committee last year was very commendable. This research board is to be charged with the duties of conducting and coordinating research and development for defence. That is another matter. Our universities are already doing some of this and there will be duplication and overlapping of work.
Then the board is to establish scholarships and make grants in aid. The universities and colleges and boards of education have done a great deal in providing aid in the Toronto district in the way of scholarships and so on. Some of these young soldiers have been unable to complete senior matriculation; they cannot get into universities, and I am glad to see that the welfare minister is trying to cure this condition and enable all to do so.
Provision is made for the salaries, remuneration and expenses of the board. If there is duplication it is going to be all board and no security or relief. We will see the result of this in the civil estimates. Wait until you see next year's estimates for this new organization. I understand the minister was a soldier and has been only two months in the depart-
National Defence Act

ment, but this whole thing should go to a committee. The resolution should be considered most carefully. It covers almost everybody-the man who enlisted in the last war, the man who enlisted in this war, the men in the different branches of the new defence services and those who may be out of the country. If a man is injured, if he wants to go to a university or if there are other things he wants to know, in many cases he will have to run down to Ottawa. I know of soldiers who have wasted a lot of money coming down here on one or two little matters which they should have been able to have fixed up at home. They wasted money on their train fare, they could not get in an hotel and when they got here they could not find out anything about what they wanted to know.
I understand there is not to be a general veterans committee this session. Veterans affairs and the care of their estates are going to be most important matters in the next twelve months, and I submit that this resolution should go to some committee made up of veterans where these different things could be considered. This is a matter in which there should be no partisanship. If the minister will agree to sending this to a select committee he will make some progress and we will be able to get on with other bills.
The other place is going to take a holiday because there is no work. There is no use taking holidays when there is work to be done. Some of those who are working today no doubt will run away and take a holiday and come back to work another day. This is a matter which a committee of this house should consider. We should be able to have the advice of the officers in the various military districts, the soldiers' organizations, the hospital officials, and so on. Once the facts are laid before us the bill will go through the house in no time at all.
Hon. members should recall the way the veterans legislation was handled1 last session. It is with deep humility that I speak on this subject because I am not a soldier. I do think that we should not go over the heads of the soldiers' organizations and pass this resolution on the eleventh day of the session. I would like to see the other government bills go through quickly and if the minister will consider between now and Monday the setting up of a small committee I think it will bring results.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: Will the minister define the meaning of the words "service estates"? Is that something distinct from the total estate of the demised soldier?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
Yes, I thought I made that clear yesterday. It is defined- by the regulations as meaning:
. . . that part of his personal estate which consists of balance of pay and allowances and other emoluments emanating from the crown, which at date of death are due or otherwise payable and effects issued by the crown, which under regulations he is permitted to retain, and all personal belongings found on the deceased and in camp, quarters or otherwise in the care or custody of the service authorities, including cash on hand and personal articles and effects.
This property is disposed of by handing it over to the executor, if the soldier has made a will and appointed an executor, or to the legatee if the soldier has made a will and has no executor, or to the administrator if one has been appointed by the courts. In other words this is simply machinery whereby the property is passed on to the next of kin or the heir or executor of -the soldier. This only applies in respect of those who are in the active forces. Soldiers who have ceased to be in the active forces and are therefore exsoldiers and who are receiving treatment from the Department of Veterans Affairs are dealt with by that department.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
A good deal of this debate could have been avoided I think had the minister made a full explanation of what was intended by the bill to follow the resolution. Without having seen the bill, and having heard only the minister's explanation, it looks to me as if his purpose in the first section of the resolution, which provides for the appointment of three associate deputy ministers, is to synchronize and unify the three branches of the service. To the extent that that is done I think the members of the house are in agreement.
With respect to the administration of service estates, I would ask the minister to give some indication whether the purpose is to save expenses to the estate, and whether, should accounts be presented against the estate during the course of its administration, the department will see to it that counterclaims by the estate against those presenting claims will not be jeopardized.
With respect to the establishment of the defence research board, one phase I think deserves commendation, and that is the establishment of scholarships and the making of grants in aid. I should like the minister to indicate to the committee whether these scholarships will be issued generally across the dominion or whether military strings will be attached to them; that is, will they be held for military personnel, or be open to the general public provided they follow a certain line of research?

National Defence Act

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
Answering the first question. the effect of handling service estates of service personnel in this way will undoubtedly be to save expenses to the beneficiary of the estate. It is done very simply and very easily. 'No provision is made to protect the claim of any claimant against the estate, because no claims may be made against the service estate of service personnel. They are exempt from seizure; therefore that question does not arise.
With regard to the establishment of scholarships by the research board, the purpose of securing power to give scholarships is to enable the board to ensure that research work is done by competent people, and in order to do that it may be necessary to train research workers or to give a fellowship to assure that a. job is done in a university or other teaching institution.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: Will the applicants for research scholarships be considered on a broad basis provided they have the required research qualifications?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: Oh, yes.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
Reverting to the original question of the hon. member for Nanaimo, this is a bill to put into statutory form an order in council respecting service estates. I can well understand that when the defence department as it now stands was set up, and the Department of Veterans Affairs was just coming into being, it might have been difficult to transfer jurisdiction over this matter from the defence department to the veterans affairs department. But here we are dealing with the administration of service estates; undoubtedly gratuities for service will be involved, and apparently this provision will apply in the case of the death of a soldier who is under the care of the veterans affairs department. Therefore it seems to some of us that this might be the time to put the order in council in statutory form and under the jurisdiction of a different department. That is the point we are raising.
In the first place, if the purpose is as the minister has just stated, simply to pass the estate over to an executor or civil administrator, no great department is required1 for that; it is a physical job. But if the job is really to administer these estates, a professional staff will be required, thus increasing the expenditure of the Department of National Defence. At a time when the economy axe is being applied to that department I think its minister would be only too glad to get rid of any expenditure that was not for the purpose of building up our future armed forces. W e
have not yet heard the minister say it would not be a better idea to transfer this jurisdiction to the Department of Veterans Affairs, and that is the point we would1 like answered.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: I am sorry I did not appear to make myself sufficiently clear. This legislation does not apply to veterans at all. It applies only to men who are in the active army and who die while in the service.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
On that argument it
might be said that the administration of pensions to widows of deceased soldiers should be under the Department of National Defence. The mere fact that they are not veterans but were in the service at the time of their death does not imply that their service estate could not be better administered by the veterans affairs department, which looks after pensions and grants and gratuities. As this provision stands, apparently the Department of Veterans Affairs will have to pay over to the Department of National Defence sums of money standing to the credit of the deceased soldier.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: That must be so if the soldier has built up any gratuities for service. We suggest that the reverse should be the case.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: Gratuities are paid by the Department of National Defence; so is pay, and the man's credit standing on his pay account when he dies is in the hands of the Department of National Defence, so that much the simplest way of disposing of it is to have someone in the defence department pay it over in accordance with the directions in bis will, or, if he has not a will, to his next of kin. Why should we in the defence department dispossess ourselves of the money and transfer it to veterans affairs, who never had anything to do with the man, in order that they might do the job?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: Could it not be done through the paymaster's branch of national defence without special legislation?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: There is a director of estates who works in close cooperation with the paymaster's 'branch and with the judge advocate general, and there is no big set-up. It is simply a device to facilitate settlement in connection with estates for service personnel who die in the service.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: I think this is a good idea; it is something which has been in effect much longer than since last August.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
Yes, that is right.
National Defence Act

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: In fact, it has been in effect for some years. It allows the department to administer only that portion of the estate of the man who has practically no other estate except such as appertains to his service. It is done without expense, and if the estate is of any size the department will not handle it. If there is insurance, for example, they do not want to handle it; they want the widow or next of kin to take it over. As I recall it, it is simply done by a solicitor of the department who understands the work, and it has been of benefit to a great number of people who had relatives who died in the last war. It will apply in the future only to a few. We do not expect, that in a comparatively small army very many will die, and as regards those who die it is a cheap way of disposing of their estates. I am not saying anything as to whether the Department of Veterans Affairs or the Department of National Defence would "best administer the estate". The act will apply only to estates that are very small and it is not an important matter.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: I am very much obliged to the hon. member for his understanding assistance.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
The question of
scholarships comes up under this resolution. Can the minister tell us how much money is involved? We approve of it, but we think some definite amount should be stated as the maximum to be spent in the matter.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: All expenses of the defence research board will be paid1 out of moneys appropriated by parliament and will be under full parliamentary control.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: It is significant that the first part of the resolution refers to the appointment of not more than three associate deputy ministers of national defence. Will the minister make quite clear whether the three branches of the armed services, as we understood them under wartime conditions, are to be continued as more or less separate and distinct branches, or is the whole sendee of national defence under one head? Are these associate deputy' ministers to have everything to do with all the different services of national defence, or will there still be a differentiation between the different arms of the service?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: The question was raised yesterday afternoon. The present intention is to have the department work as a unit with one deputy minister, the associate deputy ministers dealing with the affairs of the whole department and of all the services.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
Yesterday on the orders of the day I asked a question in regard to motor

vehicles. I intended to leave it until the minister's estimates came up for consideration, but looking at the explanatory note in the bill, I see the purpose of the bill is to amend the militia act. I suggest that when the act is amended it should take into consideration the motor vehicle belonging to the civilian, which it does not do at the present time.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: I am sorry, but at present we are discussing the resolution to amend the Department of National Defence Act, and not the item to which the hon. member refers.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: When will that come up- not under this?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: No.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister questions about two matters. First of all, this resolution refers to a defence research board and the establishing of scholarships and making grants in aid. I take it that everyone in the house is in favour of the defence research board and of giving them every possible assistance in view of the increased importance of research in matters of defence, but would the minister explain in a little more detail than he has done so far what is intended in the way of scholarships and grants in aid? Are these scholarships to be in the various universities in Canada, and perhaps abroad, and to what type of institution will the grants in aid be paid?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
Dealing first with the grants in aid, hon. members will appreciate that it would be a good thing for any defence research board to use the agencies that exist today to do research work as far as they can. There are the universities and industries and a limited number of institutions in Canada equipped to do research of any kind, including defence research, and frequently defence research has a very close association with research for civilian purposes. It will often happen that a piece of research that is being done either in an institution or in some industry could be broadened out or be specially directed so as to cover some point of research which the defence research board wishes to cover. Those are the conditions under which grants in aid will be given.
With regard to scholarships or fellowships, the answer is very much the same, but here we are dealing with the individual rather than an institution or industrial concern, and the payment would be made either to equip him to do defence research or to get him to do a particular bit of defence research work. This provision would be exactly the same as the

National Defence Act
provisions already in existence with regard to civilian research undef the national research council.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: Will the defence research board have anything to do with research into the development and use of atomic energy?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: As hon. members know, atomic energy is being dealt with under the atomic energy control board by virtue of legislation which was passed by the house last year. I should think the defence research board would be interested in any developments in that connection, but it will not have directly to do with the atomic developments.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: As the minister knows, the atomic energy control board was set up without any representation from the defence forces. Apparently there will be some connection between the work of that board and the work of this defence research board. Could some plan not be devised whereby our defence people will have a direct part in the development and use of atomic energy? Has the government in mind any such change, and if not, will consideration be given to the matter?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: Certainly, consideration will be given to the hon. gentleman's suggestion.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Kamloops suggested setting up a committee of this house on defence matters. The minister said that he would look into the suggestion and make a statement. I hope he can tell us something about that today. Something should be done along that line. It was proposed in 1945 and again in 1946, and in 1946 the Prime Minister made this answer to the suggestion as found at page 406 of the daily edition of Hansard'.
I think the suggestion of my hon. friend is a very good one and, as the Minister of National Defence has just said, it is one that he is prepared to consider sympathetically. But once again the house will have to ask itself how many committees it can stand. We are enlarging the number and it will have a bearing on the attendance in the house. I think my hon. friend's suggestion of that particular committee is a very good one.
I fully realize the weakness in having many committees. A number are set up under the rules of the house which are of no use at all. Some of the standing committees never even meet; others meet only once or twice. These committees make very little contribution to the work of the house. But I am afraid we are drifting into the position that the people and the house are losing interest in the defence problem, which is a very serious one, far more serious than it has ever been before. That is so because of the importance of the
north country and the development of new weapons, such as the atom bomb and rocket projectiles. It is therefore important that the members of this house know what is going on in order to be able to understand the problem and give support to the defence forces. If members from every party knew the difficulties in connection with building up an adequate defence, they could keep their fellow members in their party informed, and I am sure that far more generous and understanding support would be given to the defence forces. In addition, we could go out and explain to the people what steps have to be taken. As it is now, both the house and the people are largely in the dark on this question, and I am afraid that condition will become worse from year to year. It looks as if the defence department is being made to take most of the cuts demanded for the sake of economy. In any event, there is a great deal of merit in having a committee of this house on defence matters. There is one in the United States senate and house of representatives, one for the army and another for the navy. I hope the minister is in a position to say something about that suggestion.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
I appreciate the very reasonably stated suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver South. As he says, the question of defence is one of great importance and concern. I cannot yet tell the committee what the estimates will be; but when they are made available, as they will be in a few days, I hope the house and the country will be gratified by the reductions from wartime levels, just as I believe they will feel that the sum provided for is not anything like on a pre-war basis, but is appropriate to meet the defence needs of Canada at this time as well as we can.
With regard to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Kamloops that we should have a committee of this house on military affairs, I may say that since he made that suggestion again last night I have looked into the debates to which the hon. member for Vancouver South has referred. There is, of course, a very reasonable case to be made for having such a committee. However, I should state to the committee some reasons why I believe it would not be desirable, particularly at this time.
In the first place, the hon. member referred to the fact that in the United States there are committees of both houses on army and navy matters. That is or was correct, although I think there is to be some consolidation of their functions. However, as hon. members know, in the United States there is a totally different
National Defence Act

parliamentary system from that which we have. Ours follows very closely the British system; and it is a striking fact that in Britain there is no committee of parliament on military affairs or defence. It has often been discussed and suggested but it has always been decided against.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: They have none on external affairs either, have they?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
That is quite correct. I think a case can be made against having functional committees. Last year, when it was suggested that there should be a committee on health and security, I believe I made the same observations. I am still of the same view, that it is cutting across our parliamentary system to have committees on functional matters. It is based on a different concept of government than from that which we have. In the United States, as hon. members know, committees of congress have an important part and a positive role in formulating policies, and, in fact, carrying on government; whereas here that is the responsibility of the administration, and it carries out that responsibility as long as it can keep the support and confidence of the house.
Quite apart from these general remarks, I should like to point out to hon. members the rather difficult position we in the Department of National Defence are in this year. I think it is just two months ago today that I was appointed as the first minister of a single department since the war, and we decided at once to try to merge the three civil establishments in the three existing departments. In order to bring that about I thought it desirable to get the whole department, including the headquarters of the three armed services, in one physical location, and just four weeks ago we started the move from the various buildings in Ottawa in order to get the department into the three buildings on Cartier square. That has been an immense job, very creditably carried out. It had to be carried on simultaneously with the ordinary work of the department, and at a time of year when the estimates were being prepared. It has involved the physical dislocation of virtually everyone in the department. That move will not be complete for another month or more; it has to be done by steps. Then, the physical move having been completed, we will be engaged in the work of merging the civilian branches into one set of branches, and consolidating and coordinating the branches of the three services. That will be going on steadily throughout the year. This operation of establishing an organization on a sound post-war basis will take a considerable period 
of time. It is easy to speak about it; it is fairly easy to draw a blueprint of it, but it requires literally thousands of changes to be worked out in practice. If this work is to be carried on as rapidly and as effectively as I believe all hon. members would like us to do it, then it will be necessary for us in the department to give a very great part of our time and attention just to that job.
As hon. members know, the establishment of a parliamentary committee means at once that the minister and the senior officials of the department, as well as considerable numbers of the staff, become fully engaged in attending to the work of servicing the committee, securing information and that kind of thing. In a time of very quick change and development that is a difficult operation to perform, more difficult than at any other time. For that reason I believe that if a committee on military affairs is desired by the house it would be greatly preferred that it should not be introduced this year. In this matter we are in the hands of the house, which of course has control of the rules of procedure, but my hope would be that we would not have a committee on military affairs, certainly not this year.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: A few moments ago the minister stated that there would be a deputy minister and three associate deputy ministers. Can the minister say whether these associate deputy ministers will be responsible directly to the minister, or through the deputy minister of defence?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext: They will be responsible through the deputy minister of defence, but of course will have access to the minister at any time.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
Originally I did not
intend to enter this discussion, but decided to do so when the minister mentioned the standing committee on external affairs which was set up a year ago last September, at the first session of this parliament. It seems to me the relationship between the questions of external affairs and defence is now closer and more integrated than at any other stage in our national development and our national history. It took session after session before the government were persuaded to set up what we thought, and what we now know, to be a most vital standing committee in our parliamentary structure, that on external affairs. The work of that committee during the last two sessions has justified all the arguments which we had previously advanced from time to time and which I may say went unheeded by the government for a long

National Defence Act
period. So it seems to me that now, when defence is so closely connected with the whole problem of international affairs, any possible argument the minister may advance for postponing the setting up of a committee on defence is largely eliminated. Actually I do not think there is much time to be lost in setting up such a committee.
If I may say so, it is useless to argue that because they do not have such a committee in the United Kingdom we should not have one here. As an hon. member has pointed out, in the United Kingdom they do not even have a committee on external affairs. The situation in Canada was certainly emphasized in the public mind by the statement made yesterday by the Prime Minister with respect to collaboration between this country and the great republic to the south; and if ever there was a time when the public were connecting two great matters facing the Canadian parliament, those of defence and external affairs, that time is the present. I believe the minister is entirely wrong in suggesting that this question should be left over even for another session. Events do not wait, and parliament must keep abreast of events. For two sessions now we have had an external affairs committee in operation. Surely we cannot let a third session go by before the collateral committee on defence is set up, so that the work of the two committees may if necessary be coordinated from time to time.
Just before I sit down may I deal with one other matter raised by the minister-the servicing of such a committee by those in the department itself. I think that is a worn- out argument. We heard it advanced with respect to external affairs; we have heard it with respect to almost every government department. In any event, we can hardly expect a government to be very anxious to display to the public all the things that go on behind the scenes if they can avoid doing so. On the other hand1 it is the job of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition to bring out these facts so they may be appreciated by the public; because after all it is public money that keeps all these things going, not the minister's money, or mine, or yours, Mr. Chairman; it is the money of the millions of Canadian people who are paying their taxes to this government. They have a right to know the policy underlying the whole question of defence, and whether or not their dollars are being spent to the very best advantage to the country. So I say to the minister that bringing men from the defence department before a parliamentary committee in the final analysis may mean that changes in policy will come about after close investigation and study of existing problems and policies, which in the years to come may save much of the time of those in the department and at the same time save many dollars to the taxpayers in greater efficiency and1 the carrying on of public business with greater dispatch.
As I see it, in peace time the question of the servicing of a committee by departmental officials should not be raised. Surely the officials have had the experience of five or six years of war. Perhaps in those times we had a perfect right to say that these men should not be brought before a parliamentary committee except under the most extraordinary circumstances, because we were at war; but surely it cannot be argued now that the reorganization of a department should require the same amount of time, the same energy, the same attention or the same application to the task as the fighting and winning of a war itself. Still that would seem to be what the minister is attempting to suggest this afternoon; and I want to put it in the most charitable way I can with respect to him. But I do want to say, with every bit of emphasis at my command, that the experience we have had with external affairs should teach us a lesson with respect to the defence committee which is now suggested. The minister should not leave it for another year; I urge upon him that he appoint the committee before the close of the present session.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:

part of the resolution that permission is sought to provide for the salary, remuneration and expenses of the defence research board, and for a pension and superannuation fund for the benefit of employees out of moneys appropriated by parliament. Or does he propose setting up a new civil service superannuation provision under this resolution, and giving control of salaries and remuneration to a different group?

speechtext: I believe the hon. member is out of order.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
I am speaking to the
resolution. What is the purpose of the last part of it?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
Our object is to set up this board in much the same way as the national research council is set up, but on a much smaller scale, and with as little adminia-

National Defence Act
trative personnel as possible so that its top people can be free to work at planning and research. The national research council does not come under the civil service commission. I understand the national research council has not yet a superannuation fund, but it is proposed it should have one. If so, the officers and employees of the defence research board would probably make arrangements with the national research council to come under their fund, one which would probably be better suited to the needs of scientific and technical workers than would a fund operating under ordinary civil service arrangements. That is being worked out.
The expectation is that to a considerable degree the defence research board would be staffed by people seconded from other institutions or government departments, or from industry. The hope is that the board will be able to make arrangements satisfactory to the institution or branch lending the personnel, so that such people will not lose pension or superannuation benefits. Thus it will be possible to secure the services of personnel on a temporary basis to do specific jobs.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
From what the minister has said this afternoon it would appear it is now government policy to get as far away as possible from the Civil Service Act and the Civil Service Superannuation Act, to allow crown companies to form their own superannuation acts, to allow the national research council to have its own superannuation act, and, by this resolution, to allow the defence research board to form its own superannuation provisions.
We are coming to the point where on the one hand members of the civil service whom we describe as career civil servants receive their rights, privileges and benefits under one act, and persons connected with crown companies, boards and commissions receive similar or additional benefits under different acts and out of different funds. This tends fo the creation of a chaotic condition in the civil service. Members of the House of Commons, with the esteem they have for the loyalty of our permanent career civil servants and the service they have given to our country, should hesitate before they set up other institutions making provision for benefits, privileges and rights established on a different basis.
It is my belief that the government as an employee of man-power should not permit boards and commissions which operate independently of parliament to care for their employees in a better or different manner from that employed by the government in looking after its own career civil servants.

We should consider what the results may be as affecting the career man who sees the government setting up boards, crown companies, departments and commissions on a different basis, and giving their employees special privileges which the career civil servant does not have.
The minister should consider the chaotic condition and the dissatisfaction he may create if he persists in permitting this condition, under which he is getting away entirely from the Civil Service Act and drifting to the old state of political patronage-because we are heading in that direction. The political patronage and favouritism within crown companies and boards may be greater than the political patronage we had before the Civil Service Act was passed.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
As the minister knows, I suggested before the formation of a defence committee of the house. He should not have any apprehension that such a committee would upset the functioning of his department. I believe he would1 find, as did the Department of Veterans Affairs last session, that such a committee would be of definite assistance to the functioning of his department. Not only did the committee which dealt with veterans affairs bring forward many recommendations, and not only did it review all the legislation connected with veterans, but a great many suggestions for the improvement of the department were made in committee.
There is one point which must not be forgotten in the matter of defence, and that is that in the defence of this or any other country in any future war there will be less and less time to prepare. The time factor is ever shortening. Parliament's primary duty is the safety of the state. Generally the estimates for the Department of National Defence are brought down in the last days of the session, when the weather is extremely warm and members want to go home. The whole business is being rushed through perhaps in less than a day. It is impossible to get expert information. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, and through you to the house, that since the external affairs committee has been taken out of politics, since we have representation at the united nations and on other international tribunals made up of members of all the parties in this house, the matter of defence should be considered in a non-political light.
I do not believe we could have a debate on defence in this house without taking sides, and I think the day has come when we should realize that this is too vital a matter to be the subject of a partisan dispute.

National Defence Act
There is one further matter. If a committee were set up, experts and other members of the Department of National Defence and hon. members of this house could be called upon to give testimony. I am thinking of people like General Crerar, who made an important pronouncement quite recently in this city, and of men like Doctor Solandt. There could be given in the committee information which it might be considered unwise to have generally debated. If the committee knew of the new weapons and the frightful possibilities of mass destruction that are possible should another war occur, we would then have in this house a body of expert or improved opinion which would have a most salutary effect upon the debating of our whole defence programme.

They indicate that there is a feeling that things are not going as they should in the Department of National Defence. The opposition certainly are not responsible for that decision and I do not see why there should be any delay in setting up a committee such as has been suggested. As the hon. members for Vancouver South, Peel and York South have pointed out, when committees of this house have been set up to consider legislation there has been less trouble and less partisan discussion in the house than there was on other matters in connection with which the members of the opposition were 83166-25
denied information, and in connection with which sometimes the people of Canada have been denied information.
We do not know at this moment what cuts the minister has made in the Department of National Defence. We do not know whether there is to be a squadron of aircraft on both the east and west coasts. We do not know anything about the cadet situation. That is why the minister is met with these inquiries, and it is high time such a committee was set up in order that the experience of government and opposition members might be made available to the department. That is all I wanted to say on that point.
Will the minister make another statement in the near future in connection with setting up a committee? Will the minister tell the committee how the defence forces will be tied in with the research board to which this resolution refers?

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
I do not suppose there has been a resolution as important as this one which has been introduced to the committee with so few remarks by the minister in charge. I did not hear what the minister said yesterday, but on looking over Hansard I find that he has not given us much help. I should like to ask a question or two about the research board. I notice the minister said that this board will have to do with direction and coordination, but the resolution states that it will be charged with the duties of conducting and coordinating research and development for defence.
Will the minister tell the committee just what the research board intends to do? Is it to concern itself with applied science, or will it concern itself with basic science? Those two divisions in the scientific field are quite distinct. Is it to have its own facilities for research along basic lines or along applied lines, or is it merely to give certain directions to those who are conducting research along defence lines and perhaps along basic lines in other fields?
I think the committee would also like to know how much the minister appropriated in his last defence estimates for research activities or, in the alternative, how much he intends to ask for in the forthcoming estimates for this important activity. Will there be a coordination committee to work with the national research council? Why does this board have to be separate from the national research council? Will the head of the board in the Department of National Defence, Doctor Solandt. have a board of independent advisers, or will it be set up as it has been set up in the United States? I understand that in con-

National Defence Act

nection with the United States legislation certain fears have been expressed that some of the scientists appointed to their research institution have been appointed for political or patronage reasons rather than from the point of view of purely scientific knowledge. If the minister would be good enough to enlighten the committee on these general points before we have the bill in front of us I think we would all have a better idea of where we are going.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE DEPUTY MINISTERS-SERVICE ESTATES- DEFENCE RESEARCH BOARD
speechtext:
The hon. member for Rosedale referred rather caustically to the brevity of my remarks when I introduced this resolution. As he and the committee know, more resolutions are introduced without any remarks at all than are introduced with preliminary remarks. The practice since I have been here has been to have a brief statement on the resolution, which is followed by a brief debate, and the house then gets down to work on the bill, which is the most profitable way, I suggest, of dealing with the matter.
The hon. member asked how much would be appropriated for defence research. As he and the committee know, the amounts to be set. out in the estimates are first made available to parliament when the estimates are tabled by the Minister of Finance, and that will be done in a very short time.
As to the composition of the board, it is under the chairmanship of the director general of research, Doctor 0. Solandt, a person with a distinguished scientific record, especially during the war, in many fields of research. On the board, in addition to Doctor C. J. Mackenzie, president of the national research council, are the three chiefs of staff, or their representatives, representing the three services; also representatives of industry and experts in the field of research itself. The reason why the board is created separately from the national research council is that this has been found to be the best form of organization by everyone engaged in it, and has the support of Doctor Mackenzie himself. It is felt that in that way there will be much closer coordination with the armed services themselves, and through that coordination it will be more possible to keep the services research minded, which I think is a desirable aim.
Coordination with the national research council will, of course, be very close. In fact a considerable amount of research in defence matters will continue to be carried on by the national research council in close cooperation with the defence research board. I think, for example, of its work on aviation which has

had great value for civil flying as well as military. The defence research board will also carry on directly defence research activities through such agencies as that carrying on the work being done in Toronto on aviation medicine, which has also been of great value as regards not only flying in war but flying in peace.
