subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION

speechtext: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Defence) moved the second reading of Bill No. 14, to amend the Militia Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Is the minister not making any statement?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
As hon. member's know, the governing statute for the army of Canada is the Militia Act, chapter 132 of the revised statutes of 1927. The act was first enacted in 1868. It has been amended since on very few occasions. I should tell the house that we aim, just as soon as it is possible, to introduce a bill to replace the Militia Act in toto, as was done in the case of the Naval Service Act, but it will take a good many months to prepare such a bill and we would also like to have the experience of this year behind us. It will not be possible to introduce that bill at this session, but work is already being done on it.
The amendments proposed in the present bill are largely changes of a textual or drafting nature designed to bring the act up to date and to provide for the post-war organization of the Canadian army on a sound basis. Sections 1, 6, 7, 9, 10, 14, 15, 17, 18, 20, 30, 31 and 34 are almost entirely confined to making changes in the words used in order to bring the language into line with present practice. Some of the changes are the following: For "Canadian militia" we substitute "Canadian

Militia Act
army"; for "permanent force" we substitute "active force"; for "non-permanent force" we substitute "reserves". The word "corps" becomes "unit" because now thete is a military formation known as a corps, and the old expression "corps" has been replaced in common practice by the word "unit". "Military district" becomes "command"; "officer for the time being commanding the militia" becomes "adjutant general or an officer commanding a command", and the "adjutant general" becomes "chief of general staff."
Then, too, as hon. members know, when the Militia Act was enacted, means of transport available for the militia were described as- and I quote from the old act-"horses, mules, oxen or other animals". Those were indeed the horse and buggy days. Now war has become quite a different matter. Three sections of the bill-2, 23 and 28-deal with "vehicles, aircraft or other means of transportation" in addition to horses, mules, oxen or other animals. Section 3 is intended to clarify the position regarding the enlistment of boys under eighteen years of age. Section 4 takes account of the fact that when the Militia Act was enacted there was no Canadian navy or air force, in making provision for the members of these forces being exempted from service in the army. Sections 5, 6, 8, 11 and 16 deal with matters of organization and command, and sections 22, 24, 25, 29, 31, 32 and 33 deal with matters of military law and the laws applicable to the Canadian army.
With this brief explanation, I hope we shall proceed to discuss the clauses of the bill one by one. As I have explained, the changes are for the most part of a drafting or technical kind, designed to bring the language of the act into accord with present-day usage, I repeat that the reason why more fundamental changes are not made at the present time is that it is the intention as soon as possible to introduce into parliament a complete revision of the Militia Act. What we are now asking parliament to do is to make the changes necessary to carry on the active and reserve forces on the basis developed in consequence of our experience in two wars.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
The minister, in introducing the bill to the house, has given us the impression, that the amendments are only of a procedural and textual nature. I suggest to you Mr. Speaker, that that is very far from being the case, and that in this bill in several instances there are fundamental changes which need to be carefully discussed on second reading and also after we get into committee.
The first thing I have to say is this. Here was, par excellence, on second reading of the bill to amend the Militia Act, an opportunity for the minister to give the house and the country a complete statement on what has happened in the Department of National Defence and in the services since he took office two months ago. But he has not taken that opportunity.
I want to call to your attention, sir, the debate that took place only this afternoon when speaker after speaker pointed out to the minister the great advantage which would accrue to the services and to himself if he took the house into his confidence on matters affecting the army by the appointment of a defence committee. The minister has indicated that he will not appoint a defence committee this session, and that only heightens what I say is his duty, namely, to take an opportunity like this to tell us what he is doing, why he is doing it, and to enlist our support instead of incurring our criticism.
The minister said yesterday, in answer to a question, that he did not believe there was confusion in the country over the future of the cadet forces except on this side of the house. I believe that there is grave concern in the country not only about the cadet services but about the whole status of the defence forces, and) it is one and only one of a long succession of reasons why in our opinion, the country has no confidence in this government.
We have no confidence in the government because we think the government has failed in many of the things it has undertaken. We believe that this government has failed in its task of constructing a satisfactory defence force for Canada. We believe, too, that it would have been possible under a different policy to provide a satisfactory defence force within the means of the Canadian taxpayers.
If I were to try to put my finger on the basic trouble in the policy of the government, I would say it is the fact that ever since the end of hostilities there has been an uncertain purpose behind our forces and an uncertain amount of money wherewith to carry out that uncertain purpose. If there had been certainty in the government's mind as to the purpose of the post-war army they were to set up; if there had been an indication over a certain period of years of the minimum fund which the defence forces might have at their disposal, then I do not think there is any doubt that the soldiers could have designed a satisfactory force.
But if the policy remains uncertain; if the amount of money jumps around, from very large sums last year to very small sums this
Militia Act

year, and so on; if the minister intervenes even down to the size of units, instead of thinking only in terms of the whole force, then I say that the soldiers who have the military responsibility will not be able to do their job, and any force so constructed will be a weak compromise between political and military judgments. If there is concern in Canada, as many of us believe, over the future of the armed forces it is, in our opinion, because that weak compromise has occurred.
This bill gives no relief. We have had no statement of policy, and in these provisions, apart from the textual changes which the minister mentioned, I suggest that we shall find an intensifying of the sections which make for uncertainty as to the purpose and command of the force and as to the allocation of responsibility between the political head of the force and the military-head.
It is intended in the bill to repeal section 27. That section empowers the governor in council to appoint a commander of the Canadian militia. The repeal of that section will leave the minister-not a soldier, although he is a veteran-as the commander of the Canadian armed forces. That in itself is a matter we shall hope to discuss at some length when we have section 27 before us.
Having looked at the question of command for a moment, I wish to look at the army itself; and I say to you, sir, that uncertainty in policy has been the watchword since V-J day. Time after time in this house in the last two sessions we on this side pointed out the danger of continuing that uncertainty and asked the then minister, in the interests of the forces over which he had supervision, to state definitely the policy and purpose, to >et the forces know what it is they are supposed ;o do and to let the country know why we maintain armed forces. Since we did not get that statement of policy, I have always felt that we got off to a very shaky start, even in the old programme. Not only had we a lack of policy, but we had a lack of leadership of an organization which has been accustomed to good leadership, which thrives on good leadership, but which will not function without being certain of what it has to do and of its commanders.
In any event, we went along. The size of the force was set without a determination of its purpose and without any tie-in between that size and the results it was supposed to attain, and it is not surprising that it was not recruited as quickly as many of us might have wished.
Then some by-elections took place in the recess, and the government realized the truth of something we on this side of the house

had been urging all during the last session. They realized that there was a limit to the amount of money they could spend; and when they were brought to task by the people in these by-elections they started to think of economy in a w'ay they had not done before. With the thought of economy in mind on this whole matter of defence, they just wrenched the wheel hard over and brought an already uncertain programme into greater uncertainty than ever. For these reasons we must have in this debate certain information from the minister. We want to know whether this reduction of an already minimum-size force down to seventy-five per cent of what was agreed on all sides to be an irreducible minimum, w'as dictated by failure to get recruits, by economy, or by what I might call the parsimony of political panic, because there is a great deal of difference between true economy and the last expression that I uttered. We want to know also whether Canada's needs for defence are actually met by this new programme, because there are many of us who doubt whether that is in fact the case. There are many of us who believe, as I certainly do, that this reduction of twenty-five per cent from the figure set last year is dictated only by economy and without regard whatever to military necessity.
We want to know whether the responsible military officers believe that Canada's defence requirements are adequately met under the new programme. We should1 like to know whether this is a decision of the minister who commands the force or whether it is a decision of the defence council. We should like to know whether seventy-five per cent of a previous establishment will be as efficient as ICO per cent of a lesser establishment. We should like to know whether it would not have been better, in view of the need to save money, if the whole original plan had been scrapped and a new set-up employed which was within our financial means. We should also like to know how long it will be before we shall go back to 100 per cent of what was thought last year to be a minimum. If in fact, in the opinion of the government, this country cannot afford adequate national defence or cannot provide for it and at the same time have tax reductions, then we think the minister ought to tell us that. He ought to take the country into his confidence and explain that, although he would like to do much more he cannot do so for economy's sake, although he does not consider the present establishment sufficient for our defence. But it is important that we do not mislead the country into thinking that what we have is adequate if, in fact, it is not adequate.

Militia Act
Therefore in this debate we need more than just- this bill. We need a decisive declaration of policy from the minister and an explanation of the reasons behind the major changes he has made since he took over this department. Again I think it is high time that a member of this government, and preferably the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), made a statement to the country as to what is the duty of the Canadian people toward the maintenance of our armed forces. In my opinion, service in the Canadian forces is no longer the kind of hobby it was before the war. We have had from the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) cogent reasons why the first purpose of our defence forces is for the defence of our own soil. I am sure that, if the minister were to agree with him and were in this debate to tell the people that Canadians have a duty of service to their country, either in the active force or in the reserve, he would get all the men he would ever need for this or an- even larger army. I have talked to people who are concerned with getting recruits, particularly for the reserve forces. I am sure that, without a statement of that duty, we shall not get recruits in the numbers in which we could so easily get them if an appeal were made to young Canadians in the name of Canada.
I wish to say something more as to what should be the purpose behind Canada's armed forces. We have had it several times from the previous minister of national defence and, I believe, from the present minister, that no great decisions can be made until a decision has been made by the security council as to what forces will be required from Canada. That policy of awaiting the decision of the security council will just perpetuate the uncertainty which has dogged- our forces ever since the end of the war and will make the minister's problems very much more difficult indeed. Interestingly enough, I have in my hand a Canadian press report of January 30, according to which the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), who has been in New York, of course, made some comments about the security council. The minister apparently said this:
Mr. Martin reiterated Canada's view that the security council had failed to do the task entrusted to it. "The security council has been used as a propaganda agency. Our stand was that it should be a means for promoting settlement of disputes as well as a means to reduce the occasions for such disputes."
If the Minister of National Health and Welfare feels that the security council has failed to carry out the task which was allotted to it, are we to await further action by that body before deciding what kind of defence force
we should have in Canada? I say we should not. I say that the defence of Canada, the defence of Canadian shores against outside attack until our friends can come to our aid, has always been and always will be the first responsibility of the military forces of this country, and that no obligation to the united nations or to anyone else can supersede that responsibility, which is as old as history. I should like to refer to what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said in this house yesterday, as reported at page 360 of Hansard, when lie quoted what he said in reply to President Roosevelt in 193S, in these words:
We. too, have our obligations as a good friendly neighbour, and one of these is to see that, at our own instance, our country is made as immune from attack or possible invasion as we can reasonably be expected to make it, and that, should the occasion ever arise, enemy forces should not be able to pursue their way, either by land, sea or air, to the United States across Canadian territory.
The right hon. gentleman repeated that thought yesterday, on the same page of Hansard, where he said:
Each nation must therefore consider what steps it should take in the meantime to defend itself against aggression . . .
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is no longer.any need to await any decision of the security council, but that the purpose of our force is clear now and can be announced by the minister.
This very discussion I have been presenting to the house, as to where lies the dividing line between economy and military necessity, brings into clear relief one of the problems I think we should resolve before this debate is concluded. That is, what is the line of division between the military and political command of our forces. If we have a clear statement of that division of responsibility and a clear statement of the purposes of our forces, together with the assurance of at least a minimum fund for a certain period of years so that the soldiers can plan with some certainty in view of what is required of them, then I am sure that the armed forces can get away to a good start; but the time has come when we must have that statement of policy.
All those matters can perhaps be gone into in more detail when we come to the sections of the bill in committee; but I must raise one point now, a point of much more fundamental importance even than what I have been talking about heretofore. In this bill a constitutional issue of first magnitude is raised. The present section 22 of the Militia Act, which this bil! proposes to amend, places a limit on (he total number of the permanent force which may be maintained. That total number is 10,000 men. In the amendment proposed
Militia Act

by the bill before the house, there will be no limit placed by parliament on the size of the active force, but rather the size of that force is left to be determined by the governor in council. This change, were it enacted by this house, would be in breach of a convention of our constitution which has existed since the Bill of Rights in 1089; and before this debate concludes and we give second reading to the bill, we must have an assurance by the minister that this constitutional breach will be mended as soon as we get into committee. Otherwise I for one will be forced to oppose the passage of the bill.
I want to enlarge a bit upon the constitutional question here involved. By the Bill of Rights in 1689, following the revolution and bloodshed of 1688, it was determined once and for all that the army should be the army of parliament and not the army of the crown. This is the principle which is being breached by this proposed amendment. Since the war. we have had an extraordinary and alarming succession of breaches of constitutional duty on the part of this government. In the first session of the 20th parliament we started with the emergency powers act, when a bill much wider than was really needed by the government was brought in. Thereby the principle of the supremacy of parliament, which had been established since the days of the civil war in 1640. was broken. Then last February the liberty of the subject was invaded in the conduct of the spy inquiry. The order in council which invaded the freedom of the individual was based upon the emergency powrnrs act. which I have already said was too wide; and magna carta, which has been in existence since 1215, was given a great blow. Now, by this proposal the Bill of Rights of 1689 is to be abrogated. I might point out to the house that in all three of these cases these conventions of our constitution were established after bloodshed between rival parties, when it was decided that, for the preservation of our freedom and the avoidance of civil strife, it was necessary that these three principles, which have been broken by this government, should be written into our constitution for all time.
In Great Britain., as hon. members I am sure know, that practice and that constitutional principle were applied by the device of passing each year the Army Annual Act. The declaration of the Bill of Rights, namely that the raising or keeping of a standing army within the kingdom in time of peace, unless it be with the consent of parliament, is against the law, was repeated annually in the Mutiny Act, and then later in the Army Annual Act. The British House of Commons has never

been willing to leave to the crown the size of the standing army; and the raising, control and payment of the army have always been expressly sanctioned by parliament, and only for a period of twelve months at a time. In Canada, since we never had any great force, that was not considered necessary, but the constitutional principle was preserved by writing into section 22 of the Militia Act an upper limit of 10,000 which would ensure that the size of the army was always within the control of parliament.
In Canada we do not have a written constitution. as they have in the United States. We have kept it flexible and unwritten so that it could grow with the times, and we have always felt that we had a great political instrument at our service in this unwritten constitution.
It was kept unwritten and flexible so that it could evolve and grow, not so that it could be breached by any government in power at any one time. Although the opposition can point out these breaches, and will continue to do so as we have throughout this parliament, I say to the house that there is a prime responsibility upon any minister introducing a measure to ensure that his bill is within the four comers of our constitution. If that is not a responsibility of the ministry, then I am sure our constitution and our system of government will not be able to withstand attacks from within.
I am perfectly certain that in this instance there has been an oversight. I must say, however, that oversights of this importance should not be made. I assure the minister that if he will consent to the placing in this new section of an upper limit upon the size of the force, I for one will be perfectly satisfied with his undertaking so to do when we get into committee. I wish to assure him that neither I nor, I am sure, anyone on this side of the house, wants to be ungenerous in the fixing of that limit. We want to be certain that we have adequate armed forces. The figure that he is likely to name is not likely to cause any alarm on our part. But hon. members on this side of the house would be derelict in their duty if they did not call attention to this most important point, and require, before we are asked to vote, that a change be made. If we have that assurance we can go on in committee to the other important points of policy and command which I have outlined to the house. Therefore I shall say no more at the moment.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say at once that I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-

Militia Act
Burrard (Mr. Merritt) when he says that when motion for second reading was made a comprehensive statement should have been given as to the policy which lies behind this bill. I believe that opportunity should have been seized, particularly since the minister is aware that both at this session and at the last one a great deal of attention has been given by various members to the matter of defence. I believe it would have facilitated and probably shortened debate, had we had a comprehensive statement at the outset, so that we might have understood the policy behind the bill.
It seems to me that this opens up the whole matter of Canada's defensive system. This is really Canada's defence bill, which is now to be amended in a good many particulars. It is perhaps true, as the minister has suggested, that in many respects amendments to the Militia Act are largely technical. But no matter how technical some of the amendments may be, there are others which involve matters of policy. This afternoon, for example, the hon. member who has just taken his seat discussed-briefly, it is true-the relationship of our defence forces with the united nations organization. Yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made a statement to parliament involving not only the whole matter of the defence of our own country, but the defence of the region in which we live-the whole problem of North American defence. Hence in my opinion the minister would have been well advised to have made a comprehensive statement regarding suggestions for the improvement of the department over which he presides.
I wish to take this opportunity to say something about the defence of the region in which we live, and to comment upon some of the statements made yesterday by the Prime Minister. I welcome the statement that anything we do in Canada must be based upon the united nations, and particularly upon the arrangements that are to be made with the security council for the preservation of peace. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard has said, it is perfectly true that there has been considerable disappointment that the security council of the united nations has not been able to assemble the military staffs of the united nations-that is, the general staffs of the five principal powers-and to have come to some conclusion regarding the taking of effective precautions for the preservation of world peace.
I was proud of the fact that at New York the spokesman for the Canadian delegation, the present Secretary of State for External
Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) was the first representative of any nation at that assembly who drew attention to this fact, urged upon the security council the necessity for fulfilling the obligations which had been imposed upon it by the charter, and urged that immediately the responsibility should be carried out, that the general staff should be assembled, that a plan should be laid down and that an appropriate agreement should be negotiated with each of the fifty-one-later fifty-four-nations involved. This has not yet been done. Nevertheless I think that whatever we do in the matter of defence we must do in the light of our obligations under the united nations charter. And, may I add, the sooner that can be done, the better it will be for all of us; because I do not think anyone living in the world as it is today can fail to recognize the need for preparedness for any eventuality which may arise.
On the other hand, no one living today can view, except with misgiving, the tremendous amount of money and of productive effort to that extent wasted, which is being expended on armed forces, when it might be used for the building of our society, the building of homes and the provision of a better condition of life for the people in every country of the world.
Consequently I think it is to the advantage of everyone in Canada that our government continue to press upon the united nations organization, and particularly upon the security council, the necessity for speedily carrying out the provisions of the charter it is obligated to carry out in connection with international security and peace.
Having said) that, I wish to turni for a few moments to the Prime Minister's statement of yesterday. It was a very important one. I do not suppose a more important statement has been made to the house for some time. Certainly it is in many respects the most important made at this session of parliament thus far, because it brings before us the whole problem of Canada's relationship to the great country to the south and, perchance, in the minds of some, the possibilities of our relationship with the great country which is right across the pole from Canada. Consequently we must endeavour to get from the government exactly what this declaration means. I submit that in some respects it is a reorientation of policy. In days gone by, we always regarded Canada as being part of the British commonwealth of nations; we still do, and any defensive plans we establish should be more or less related to the military policies of Great Britain and the commonwealth. We now have a statement made to the house which
Militia Act

indicates clearly and perhaps realistically that the problem now is largely the integration of our defence forces with that of another great nation on this continent.
It is proposed that we go a long way in regard to that integration. It is suggested that there be an interchange of selected individuals so as to increase the familiarity of each country's defence establishment with that of the other country. If we are to do that with one country we ought to do it with other countries that may be involved in the defence of North America. After all the United States and Canada are not the only two countries in North America. To my mind, it is regrettable that we have to consider this before we are in a position to consider our obligations to the security council and to the united nations.
Then we are to have general cooperation and exchange of observers in connection with exercises and with the development and tests of material of common interest. That, of course, is to be expected under the arrangement that has been made. But again I suggest that we should follow a different policy. We should follow the policy which, I understand, was followed in connection with some other northern exercises and not only invite observers from the United States, or have them invite observers from the Canadian forces when they are held in Alaska, but invite representatives of the other powers. That was a policy followed in connection with the northern exercises held, I believe, two years ago. There are other great powers interested in all kinds of Arctic development. France is still one of the great powers and our associations with France are very close.
Then we are to have the encouragement of common designs and standards in arms, equipment, organization, methods of training and new developments. It is said that, since certain United Kingdom standards have long been in use in Canada, no radical change is contemplated or practicable and that the application of this principle will be gradual. May I say immediately that in the preparation for modern war a nation the size of Canada could not in its own factories and of itself provide all the varied types of equipment that would be needed. Consequently standardization is logical, but if we are to have a united nations organization, a security council acting for the protection of the world with force behind it to ensure peace, then I submit that we should consider standardization on a much wider scale than merely - between the United States and Canada. There should be standardization for the security force.

Parliament did know about it and parliament did not censure the government when the announcement was made to the house. As I say, we did not give that permission to Great Britain in 1937 and I do not think we should give that permission to the United States in 1917. That is the point I was making. Whatever is done under this joint defence plan should be entirely within the control of this parliament, of Canada herself. We are still a nation.
I hope that this integration of defence forces will not mean that we are to be controlled to any extent by either the ambitions or policies of our great neighbour to the south. We have the highest respect for the United States, but we were a long time in getting rid of control by Downing street and I do not

Militia Act
want to see Washington substituted for Downing street. Let us see that we do not have United States control of our country.
We must maintain complete independence of action. I believe that we should do nothing in this regard to weaken our contacts with the other commonwealth countries. There is a disposition in some quarters of this country at the present time to look toward the United States instead of to our old associations within the commonwealth of nations. As economic and social developments go forward in western Europe we may note once again, as we did in 1849, that certain people are looking to the United States rather than to the old associations because of their own economic interests.
With regard to the statement made yesterday, I am not sure whether the timing was as good as it might have been. We know there are suspicions among the nations and the announcement that was made yesterday in Washington and Ottawa may create further suspicions. I hope not. I do not think these suspicions would be well founded, but we have to do everything we possibly can to see to it that we do not give cause for suspicion. This should not give cause for suspicion, because in doing what was done yesterday Canada did everything within the orbit of the charter itself. Those familiar with the charter will know that under it regional arrangements for security may be made, provided that they are reported to the secretary-general of the united nations and circulated among the member nations. Consequently, what was done yesterday was done in accordance with the charter and should not give rise to suspicion. But in the state of the world today, policies of this nature may give rise to suspicion, and I am wondering whether the timing was as good as it might have been. Suspicion, as I said a moment ago, pervades the international scene. Again may I repeat that we should let it be known to the world that what we do with the United States in regard to the standardization of equipment and the exchange of personnel and as regards every other matter involved in this understanding, we are prepared to do with all the nations of the world within the organization of the united nations and under the security council.
We noted with a good deal of interest a short time ago Field Marshal Montgomery's visit to Moscow and his invitation to the Soviets for an exchange of certain types of personnel. That was all to the good, and I am sorry that the Soviets did not see fit to accept that invitation and arrange for mutual exchange, because I think it might have been beneficial to an understanding between these 83166-26
great powers. But our principle must be as far as possible to relate the plans we are making to the united nations.
Just a word about the bill itself. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard has well made the point to which I intended to draw attention immediately, that the size of our forces will no longer be limited under the provisions of the amending bill before us, and1 I agree with all that he had to say on that point. Parliament must not give up the right of complete control of the army. It is an age-old right and we must retain that control to the fullest possible extent.
The other point is this, that in this bill, in the event of an emergency, the calling up of men to defend the country is still left entirely in the hands of the governor in council. We know that has been the law, I was going to say for years, but in reality it is for centuries, ever since the right was taken to call out the male population against raids by Indians or other threat of danger. I believe, however, that the time has come when the right of the governor in council to call out the now large male population of Canada on any basis laid down in this bill or in any other bill should be subject to the direction of parliament, and that, before it is put into effect-there is no reason why the active forces and reserves should! not be called together in an emergency-parliament should be summoned at once and the power to conscript, because that is what it really is, should be in the hands of parliament. The governor . in council should act with the authority of parliament and only with that authority. That,
I think, is a reasonable provision which should be in any such bill.
I had one or two other matters of minor importance I was going to raise but I can do that in committee. Before I sit down, may I express the hope that the minister will introduce a complete army act for Canada. References are made in this bill to the army act as in effect in the United Kingdom, but we live undter different conditions from those in the United Kingdom; our disciplinary needs are different from theirs, and the sooner we can have our own army act controlling our own army enacted by this House of Commons, the better it will be for all concerned.

Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation at the beginning of my remarks in referring to the

Militia Act

constitutional question, which was brought up by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) this afternoon, and in that regard I should like to read one paragraph from the "History of the Forces":
But the raising, government, and payment of the army have always been expressly sanctioned by parliament, and only for a period of twelve months at a time, so that it is a statutory, and not a prerogative force, and the crown is under the necessity of annually asking for the consent of parliament to its maintenance.
Before the last session, of parliament, the then minister of national defence made a pronouncement at the Canadian club at Ottawa with reference to the armed service, and in the course of his speech he made this statement:
As I announced a short time ago, the initial organization for our post-war army will proceed on the basis of a plan which contemplates a permanently embodied force immediately available to meet minimum peace-time obligations.
And later on, he said:
The Canadian army will consist of an active force of approximately 25,000 and a reserve force of six divisions, with a total authorized strength of approximately 180,000.
We know that in the last two months we have had a new Minister of National Defence, and I bring this matter up in connection with the constitutional question involved in the amendment now before the house. This parliament approved the plan as outlined by the then minister and voted the money for the maintenance of a force of the size indicated. The present minister took office two months ago, -and since that time the force has been slashed and the security which some men thought they had when going into the reserve army and into the permanent force or active army has gone by the board. In doing that, the minister has flouted the will of parliament, and therefore, if we allow these amendments to go through as they are printed today, we shall be putting more power into his hands than has ever been put into the hands of any minister of militia in the past.
Let me ask the minister this question: What has occurred in the last year that has made such a change of policy necessary? Have the world problems eased? Is it because he cannot get men? Why is it, that, in spite of the fact that parliament approved the army requested, he has made these cuts? I am sure that the people of Canada do not know to what extent these cuts have been made.
You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that the then minister of national defence said that he desired1 to have a reserve army of 180,000, and the money vras granted by parliament for that purpose. I have in my hand the new establishment of one of the outstanding units in

Canada, whose members gave excellent service in two wars. It is a remarkable document. The total strength of privates is cut down to sixty-six men, and it may be interesting to see how those sixty-six privates are to be employed. Three of them are at battalion headquarters; twenty-six, headquarters company, the majority of whom are signallers; and the remainder are in the support company, including the mechanical drivers. In the rifle company, which is the fighting arm of the regiment, there is no allowance for any privates at all. They start off at the rank of corporal. How does a man become a corporal if he is not a private in the first place? I suggest that, in! view of this establishment the minister should explain to the house the establishments of all regiments throughout the country.
In my opinion, it is a serious matter at a time when the ex-minister of national defence pleaded with men to go back into the reserve army and build up t-heir regiments, that they should have no security, the government having cut everything from beneath their feet. The fact is that officers, non-commissioned officers, do not know whether they will have a regiment or not, and when it comes to summer camps, the only people who will be on. the strength to go to the camps will be officers and non-commissioned officers. Who will do the batman's job and: look after latrines, cookhouse fatigue, and all the other activities that go with camp life? I submit that the minister ought to make a statement during this debate, telling us why it has been deemed necessary to make these cuts to the extent that he has.
I cannot see any use in passing this bill in its present form if. directly parliament prorogues, the minister takes complete power over the armed forces. It seems to me, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard said, that the minister is now constituting himself the commander in chief of the Canadian forces, and when you make a politician commander in chief it is a very serious matter.
I wonder if the minister can give us some -idea about the ability of the Dominion of Canada to carry out its obligations in relation to the united nations organization and its undertakings under the mutual arrangement which the Prime Minister announced yesterday afternoon. The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), speaking in this house the other day, said that in case of war it would take a minimum of six months to prepare a division for action. I would say to the minister now that, under present conditions, you would not get a division in a year, because in the first place there would be no trained privates

Militia Act
in the Canadian army, and they are the men who will be needed. It is all very well to say that we can train the officers and noncommissioned officers, but the minister knows that the men in the ranks have also to be trained. He served in the army and he knows that you cannot have an army without privates in the ranks, because eventually it is the private who has to get down and hold the ground that has been won.
The minister's action since he has taken control of the department, would lead me to think he was put there for a definite purpose and that was to cut the militia and the permanent force down to the level at which it stood before the war, if not lower. Does he realize that a great deal of work has been done in M.D. No. 2 to build up a reserve army? It has taken a great deal of persuasion to get officers, non-commissioned officers and men back to their old units to keep the regiments going.
Here is a unit-and it is not the only one in M.D. No. 2 that is in this position, because they are all the same-with three hundred to four hundred men on their strength, which will have to have a muster parade and muster out fifty per cent of their men. I would ask the minister whether he thinks that is playing the game with the men who are trying to build up the forces, devoting their time and spending their money in the interests of the country. If he wants to destroy the Canadian army and the reserve army, I know of no better way of doing it. I have no doubt that the treasury board has had something to do with this action. Treasury board officials seem to be able to go into any department of government, regardless of whether we in parliament voted money for some special purpose, and say, "You cannot have the money".
I would ask the minister to explain to us why the money that we made available last year is not available for the purpose for which it was voted.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend, in my speech tonight, to make any mention of the removal of military headquarters from Calgary to Edmonton, but in view of the statement made by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe), I should like to direct his attention to my speech during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. If he will read what I said he will find that his remarks tonight could not have been more wrong. I advocated that this matter should be considered and that the move should not go forward chiefly on the ground of economy, to save several hundred thousands of dollars of the taxpayers' money rather than ask the government to spend more money. It is a sad commentary on defence matters that a member of the C.C.F. party should rise in his place here tonight and, when he is supposed to be speaking on the second reading of the bill to amend the Militia Act, should have devoted most of his time to carping at members in our party, at certain officers and at the wives of certain judges, and so forth. If that constitutes criticism or has anything to do with the amendments to the Militia Act I need to go back to school.
I should like to elaborate on certain points which have already been brought to the attention of the house by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) and the hon. member for York South (Mr. Cockeram). The bad effect on recruiting and on morale in the reserve force which has been brought about chiefly by the lack of any definitely stated government policy on defence has been mentioned. Not long before I came to Ottawa, I attended a conference of commanding officers of the reserve units in Calgary which took in all the commanding officers in southern

Militia Act
Alberta, and last Friday and Saturday I attended the meetings of the artillery association here in Ottawa. I was disappointed and discouraged to find that the general attitude amongst those officers representing a very large number of units was that, unless the government came out very soon with a definite statement of what their defence policy is and kept reiterating it in order to convince the people of Canada that a defence force, particularly a reserve force, is necessary, we would soon have no reserve force. Nearly all those officers were experiencing tremendous difficulty in recruiting, and a large proportion of them were almost prepared to give up. Their attitude was: If the government does not want this, all right; why should we go ahead and spend time and money on it? If they do not want it, let them say so. They wanted a statement of government policy which would convince particularly the young men of the country that such a force is necessary. Then, they said they could get the young men to join, but until that is done they said they cannot get them in. I would urge the government, as numerous other speakers have done, to make a definite pronouncement on defence policy, and if they want a reserve force let them say so and encourage the men to join it.
In addition to the bad effect on the reserve force that the lack of a government statement of a defence policy has caused, there is also the bad effect on the active service forces, for two reasons. First, the members of the active service forces do not know what their function is or where they are heading. Secondly, the chopping about and changing of plans which has been going on during the last two months has produced a feeling of insecurity and discouragement on the part of both officers and men. The announcement of the minister that the active forces were to be cut to three-quarters of their previously authorized strength could have no other effect than one of discouragement and insecurity. Since that announcement was not accompanied by an explanation of how this twenty-five per cent cut in man-power was to be made, the feeling of insecurity was deepened. As I understand it, some of the establishments were already up to full strength in the ranks, and the men naturally wondered what was going to happen to them. To allay this feeling of perturbation which exists in the active forces, I think the minister should tell us how it is proposed to make this twenty-five per cent cut in manpower. Are some authorized units to be done away with altogether, or are all authorized units to be recruited only to three-quarters of their strength, or is there to be a combination
of these two ways in which the reduction might be made? In any event, what is the pattern or principle that is to be followed?
Particularly I should like to know what is to happen to the brigade group which we heard so much about last session. It was to be a strong and highly mobile force, well trained and well equipped, Which would be ready to move into action almost at a moment's notice. Is that brigade group washed out altogether? Or is that also to be cut down to three-quarters of its strength? That would mean that it would not be able to work effectively. Anyone who has had any experience in fighting knows how difficult it is to carry out a task which is a battalion's task, be it attack or anything else, if you have only three-quarters of a battalion to do it.
The feeling of uncertainty which exists is also found to be causing a great deal of waste effort in the active forces. That, of course, means a loss of time and money. Last spring it was announced that every reserve force unit was to be recruited up to strength and that they could take all their men with them to camp. Shortly before I came to Ottawa, every reserve force unit, in our area at any rate, got notice that they could take to camp only a minute portion of their men. My own regiment with an authorized strength of 800 was authorized to take only twenty officers and men to camp. 'And so it went. The active forces must, during the past several months, have been making plans and administrative arrangements for the training of these reserve forces; but now that the numbers to be trained are suddenly and drastically reduced, it means that the time spent in formulating these plans has been wasted. Since arriving in Ottawa, I understand that a still further change has been made. The result is that the reserve forces do not know where they stand, and a great deal of the time and efforts of their officers has been just wasted. So much for that.
One objection I have to this bill is on general principles, in that it makes the minister the general officer commanding the militia. In the act as it has stood to date, such an officer is provided for, but in actual practice, so far as my knowledge goes, such an officer has not been appointed in recent years, and the fact that he was not appointed has been a defect in our present system. It resulted in orders being issued from several sources and in confusion and a multiplicity of red tape. In the army no one knows at the present time who is the actual head of it, and no one knew during the war. The chief of the general staff issues orders in connection with certain matters such as training and opera-
Militia Act

tions, and other officers issue administrative orders of various sorts. Which officer is the head of the army or whether the minister is the head of the army is an open question, and it is time that that situation was brought to an end. Take the case of orders being issued at the battalion level. What confusion would arise if you had the adjutant issuing certain orders and the quartermaster issuing his own orders and the medical officer issuing his own orders, and so forth! When orders are issued by the commanding officer of the battalion the result is correlation, and confusion with its attendant difficulties is avoided. If in a battalion you had the situation which prevails at army headquarters you would have the adjutant ordering the company to report for training three miles away at nine o'clock on Monday morning, the quartermaster ordering them to report at nine o'clock in connection with stores, and the medical officer ordering them to report at the same time for medical inspection and so forth. In other words, you would have a mess, and in many ways that is what we have now, confusion and difficulties of all kinds.
The present amendment, in doing away with the position .of general officer commanding, also changes certain provisions of the act so that the minister will discharge many of the functions which should be carried out by the army commander. It seems to me that this will involve making politics the overriding consideration in army matters, which ought to be as completely as possible removed from politics.
It has been an accepted principle for many years in this country that the military services and the civil service should be completely divorced from politics, but this amendment seems to be a complete reversal of that very proper concept. It provides for powers to be exercised by the minister which make him the military head of the army, thus inviting political interference in military spheres where such interference should not exist.
In that connection, I have here a brief entitled "Thoughts on the Command and Administration of the Canadian Army," which expresses clearly and in better terms than I can some of the ideas with reference to this subject which I should like to put on record. I quote:
I doubt whether one could get from the government today a clear statement as to where the command of the army rests.
Until within the last half century in Great Britain there was a commander in chief responsible to the secretary of state for war for everything which pertained to the army. The government of the United Kingdom substituted for the commander in chief an army council, which collectively commands the army.

In Canada we have imitated the outward appearance of the United Kingdom set-up, but that is all.
Further on:
It would be possible, as in Great Britain, to have an army council in command in which case the orders are issued in the name of, and with the authority of. the army council, and should be signed by the secretary of the army council.
This is not the case in Canada, to outward appearances, at least. There are only two possible alternatives. One is that there is no one actually in command and that the four senior staff officers issue orders on their own authority and in their own name, getting along together as best they can. The other alternative is that, while it may not be openly so stated, actually the minister exercises the power of command without accepting in full the responsibility for it.
The situation is not clear, plain or frank, right at the outset. Ostensibly the army council commands the army, but in actual practice the minister does.
I quote further:
Political command is had, as has been demonstrated many times in many countries, but it is not as bad as uncertainty as to who actually does effectively command. Anyone with any sound military knowledge and capacity for observation who served for any length of time at national defence headquarters in Ottawa during the war would, I think, agree that delays, vacillations, passing the buck, reluctance to accept responsibility and lack of any clear-cut policy on any large issue were the rule rather than the exception.
Political command is not bad because politicians are bad-
Many of us will be glad to hear that.
-or because they are incapable. They are as good and as capable as people likely to be found in the army or in other professions. Political command or control in detail of the army is bad because the army must always necessarily be of secondary importance to the politician. A member of the House of Commons-

I think there is a great- deal of truth in the passages I have quoted, and it is time that the anomalous situation in which we have been for many years should be cleared up. Let us be straightforward and honest about the matter. Let us have either a commander in chief or an- army council which actually commands the army, or, if the government supported by parliament wishes to have the army commanded by the minister, very well. Let us say so frankly. But do not let us have the situation we have been in for years, in- which the army generally felt, and believed it had grounds for the suspicion, that in many matters the minister actually was the army commander and that political considerations were being used to push the army and the military men about.
Perhaps one of the greatest evils, one of the greatest destroyers of morale in any army is the feeling of lack of trust in the commander, lack of trust in the government as far as the conduct of the army is concerned; and that is the situation which I am afraid we have had to a great extent and one which, when we are amending the Militia Act, we have an opportunity to get rid of.
I have another criticism of these amendments. It is that in some cases a legislative power is delegated by the act to the governor in council or to the minister. The act has been so drawn as to perpetuate in defence matters government by order in council or ministerial regulations, which we have had to submit to in time of war but which, I think, all believers in democracy are now trying to get rid of. Most of us consider that we have had enough government by order in council and ministerial regulations. Let us put the powers back into the hands of parliament where they belong and keep them there, instead of delegating some and making the situation worse than it has been.

Mr. Speaker, with your permission I shall take a few moments to address myself to these problems of defence as they affect the Canadian air force. Before I do so, I should -like to say a word to the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe). However, I see he is not in the house at the moment, so I will not bother.
First, may I say that I hope I shall in part answer his criticism that there are no policies forthcoming from the Tory party. In saying that, may I also refer him to the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) and many other hon. members on this side of the1 house, which have been most constructive.
As I see this problem of national defence, it is imperative that the government should immediately prepare an appreciation of what defences Canada needs; once they have done that, they should then endeavour to tailor their conclusions to the size of Canada's pocket. The government must have a clear idea of the role and the aim the defence forces have and of their interdependence. In other words, those of us who served in this war know the army cannot fight in these days without an air force and without supplies. We know the navy cannot sail without an umbrella. We in turn know the air force is in a hopeless position unless its main base is defended by the other forces. I suggest that the government should charge the able men of its defence forces who have served in this war actively, with the task of preparing a real military appreciation of the defence- problems of this country, and then endeavouring to put their conclusions into operation for the good of Canada; and I should include there, in order to fulfil our proper commitments to the united nations. As I see it at the present time, putting it in political language, Canada has decided) to take a free ride at the expense of the United States and the United Kingdom.
My colleague the hen. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) mentioned leadership and the importance of leadership. Mr. Speaker, as a returned man and as a former soldier, you will appreciate that without leadership a force is useless. As we go back into history, we find that the leadership and discipline of the Roman legions once secured an empire for them and secured the peace for many long years. The defence forces of Canada are incapable of fulfilling any task if they are not led; they are incapable of fulfilling any task if they are not first given the task, then the example, and finally the opportunity to do the things they know should be done. Leadership should come from the heads of these services and go down through them to the officers and non-commissioned officers. Through you, Mr. Speaker, may I say directly to the minister that if any of the heads of our services are not leading, are not representing directly to him the things which they feel are best for their forces and for the defence of Canada, they should be removed. If these men cannot lead, if they are overcome with political considerations or are overridden by timidity when they approach the government, they are not fit for their jobs. No man would want anyone on his staff who was not able and capable and who did not have the courage to express an independent opinion. If there are such men at the head of our services today in Canada the
Militia Act

government, and the minister in particular, should dismiss them. If there are any senior officers who are not capable of presenting a true and accurate picture to the minister, and of leading their forces, they should be dismissed. I am not speaking of anybody in particular. I have no one in mind when I say this. My only thought is that the forces must be led and must be given a policy to follow.
The hon. member for Calgary East also mentioned the necessity of continuity of plans. In dealing with that, may I say that the minister has in his Department of National Defence vast numbers of men; he has a tremendous machine, a tremendous organization. No businessman would step into a new business and completely tear it apart with one stroke. He would adopt the proper system, which would be gradually to change its policy without tearing off the cylinders of a working engine. That is evolution, and that is what should have happened as far as the defence forces of Canada are concerned. The whole new scheme should have been allowed to evolve, instead of allowing a major operation to be performed on the moving body of the defence forces of Canada.
With regard to the Royal Canadian Air Force, we want to know and the country wants to know just what is to be left after this twenty-five per cent reduction. I have been told, and I believe on good authority, that we need an air defence force in Canada of at least 24,000 men. That is not an arbitrary figure. As I understand it, with a force below that figure we have nothing that can be called an efficient air force. If we have that figure, we have the skeleton, the framework of an efficient one. There are many things that we in Canada need as far as an air force is concerned. We need duplication. We have to have two of everything. We have to have exactly similar forces, or almost exactly similar forces for the east coast and for the west coast. Those two similar forces should in both cases look northward toward our polar regions. We must have army cooperation. As any man who served in the army will know, the air force did a good job for them in this last war with their tactical air force and their fighter cover. We must have a force that will work with the navy, and that applies to both coasts. We must have a transport force and a reconnaissance force. We must have photographic machines, bombers, fighters and, above all, we must have an efficient staff on which to base such a force.
The country does not know how many squadrons there will be in Canada or what the roles of those squadrons will be. The

people do not know where the aircraft are to be obtained. They do not know whether they will be the newest type in design or whether they will be antiquated machines; and, as was mentioned yesterday, they do not know whether Canada will be part of the producing machinery of any standardized arms to which we should agree. To me that is a most important point. I am afraid Canada's present position ties her defence forces to the production machinery of other countries. I feel that we should have within our own country the means, to the extent we can develop them, for producing our own armaments; and if we are to standardize on United States or British types, we should be producing. The auxiliary squadrons of this country are inter ested in what type of equipment they are to have. They are also interested in learning when they are to be paid, when the minister and his department are to pay the officers so that they can begin supporting their squadrons.
Then we come to the position of cadets. As I understand it, a tremendous air cadet programme has been developed. These boys have been promised flying lessons; they have been promised camps; they have been promised equipment on which to learn. I believe now that these cadets are to be taken out of the secondary schools and the whole programme is to be curtailed so that perhaps one in a thousand will get air training, the thing they want. The leaders of the air cadet movement in Canada have been allowed to go out among their squadrons and make promises to young people, which promises are not to be kept. So that I hope we may have an early statement from the minister as far as the cadets in Canada are concerned, because I am sure neither the minister nor I shall be fit to fight another war, and it is the younger people who will have to do it.
The hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) also dealt with the problem of morale. If I could make a comment on that now, it would be that the recent changes in the Department of National Defence have gone a long way toward taking away from our defence forces the finest quality any defence force can have; that is, high morale. They are not being led; they do not know where they are going, and their morale has been sapped.
I should like to ask the minister one thing having to do with equipment. In some ways it has to do with war assets also, but I shall not enter upon that phase of it because I am sure you, Mr. Speaker, would stop me if I did. During the last war, as I understand it, we in Canada purchased all our own aircraft

Militia Act
and all our own equipment in addition to paying our forces. At the end of the war we brought back to Canada a few Lancaster bombers; but, so far as I know, they are the only paid-for machines that ever returned to this country. I am very much interested to learn what happened to the many aircraft Canada paid for and why they were not brought back to this country to be sold through War Assets Corporation, or to be broken up so that the equipment could be used for future training or farmed out to universities and air cadet squadrons.
I have practically finished, except to make one further comment. Apparently there is one member of the government who does know something about the defence of Canada, though I know that one member is fully occupied with the problems of his own department, which is the Department of Labour. At page 326 of Hansard he said:
If you have something that the other fellow wants and you are not prepared to defend it, you will lose it.
There is a very clear statement of what we are driving at today. We do not want to lose what we have here, and we are prepared to defend it. We want a government that is also prepared to defend it.

Mr. Speaker, tonight we have been discussing the instrument of national defence, so-called. I think it can be stated that in our experience of the past when we have run up against the crisis of war we have always been prepared for the last one. In other words, at the time of world war I we were prepared1 for the Boer War. When world war II broke out we were prepared for world war I. As things stand at the present time. I would say that the General Braddoeks have the situation well in hand.
The net result of world war II was that every army established on the basis we are now discussing wound up behind barbed wire fences or sitting on a beach. It was tragic and nearly cost the democratic nations of the world their freedom. But during that war instruments were forged, through necessity, that still work efficiently. I am speaking of the people's armies that were in the fields of Great Britain armed with shotguns, pitchforks and old spears to protect them from airborne invasion, the people who guarded buildings against air attack, from fire bombs and so on. I should mention also the underground of France, the civilians of Warsaw and especially those gallant Greek guerillas who defeated the Germans by their own efforts, using German equipment that they captured with their own
hands. The entry of the British army at the end of the war was unnecessary from the point of view of driving out the Germans. Now these instruments which were created out of necessity have been done away with, and once more we are building up our defence forces on the same old basis; and I imagine we are to suffer the same experiences.
We should be building up our forces for national defence around the factory and the field, because the next attack will be airborne. This "expedition frigid" or whatever it is called up in Alaska, has found that it is impracticable to move land equipment through those regions. Electric wire snaps like kindling; tires chip away to nothing in the intense cold. So we are going to be subjected in the event of war, to air attack, and all our cities are open to it. No preparation is being made to defend our people. Under our present civilization, we either live like rooks in a rookery or like rabbits in a rabbit warren. We are stuffed into huge centres willy-nilly and the government refuses to put through a decent housing programme. as is well known, with no preparation being made for decentralization of the economy. In no sense could this be called national defence from the point of view of safeguarding the lives of the people or safeguarding the machinery of production that eives us the standard of living we have today. We are repeating the mistakes of the past.
Now we are to be thrown upon the mercy of Uncle Sam; he is going to help us defend ourselves. This agreement that has been entered into could very easily be the Munich of 1947. and this with no understanding of what the situation may be in the United States tomorrow. Their political structure is unstable; it is riven with race hatred, even class hatred, as much as in any country in the world today. The general drift of our time has been toward forms of dictatorship. If they had masses of unemployed in that country, who could stop the leaders of that nation from leading them into an imperialistic adventure? That country has the most backward political leadership in the world today, and it is trying to ram down the throats of the rest of the world, against its will, a method of trade that was antiquated fifty years ago. The United States is the only country in the world having that conception of world trade, and its people are bringing confusion to the rest of the world by their antics.
United States military strategists do not stand out, and United States military analysts are still trying to outmanoeuvre the Seminole Indians. They are depending upon wealth, and wealth alone: and today wealth is a poor
Militia Act

substitute for ideas. Wars of the past have been imperialistic, in the sense that those who fought them wanted more land areas. But wars of the future are going to be wars of ideas. The country to the south of us is bankrupt when it comes to ideas. If we are going to defeat our enemy today, we must disarm him by producing a higher faith among our people in our institutions than we have at present.
We have educated people; we have highly developed resources.

Mr. Speaker, if a feeling should exist that this debate has rambled over a wide field I suggest it is because the minister has failed to take advantage of the opportunity given him today to make a clear statement on defence policy.
I feel he should have taken advantage of that opportunity because he must know that the country as a whole is anxious to have such a statement. This afternoon he did make a brief statement which contained one important fact, namely, that he and his department were considering introducing a Canadian army act in the near future. It is high time that such an act was introduced. Canada has reached the stage in her national development where she should be free to govern her own forces. She has adopted a naval code of her own and it is time that she had her own army code. It is quite conceivable that regulations passed under the army act of Great Britain might be repugnant to Canada and, if the Canadian parliament were not in session, we would have to conform to those repugnant regulations.
However, the new act is not ready, and in the meantime the minister has submitted a series of amendments to the existing Militia Act in an effort to bring that act up to date by changing the nomenclature of the various units and providing for the speeding up of the putting into effect of regulations which might be made. The minister pointed out that the majority of these amendments are of a trivial nature and I suggest that there was no necessity to put these trivial amendments through at the present time. They could have stood over until the Canadian army act was produced.
But there is one amendment which is of fundamental importance, an amendment which challenges the very structure of our government and our democratic institutions. I refer to section 22. As was brought out clearly by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt), in ancient days the armies of Great Britain were raised at the will of parliament or of the king as the case might be. After the motherland had been through several years of civil war and had experienced the restoration of the Stuart dynasty, there was a clash of interests and certain minority groups had to be protected. In. the reign of King James II, an attempt was made by the reigning monarch to introduce armed forces without the consent of parliament. There was a struggle over the Bill of Rights in the seventeenth century. That Bill of Rights laid down that armed forces should not be maintained in peace without the consent of parliament.
That was one of the fundamental principles for which our forefathers fought and died and that is one of the freedoms which we feel should be protected today. It is one of the freedoms which grew out of the struggles in bygone days. After all, our democratic institutions represent the results of struggles which date from early days. As a result of that particular struggle, such bills as the mutiny bill, the annual army act and so on were introduced into the mother of parliaments. These defined clearly year by year, for twelve months only, the size of the force which could be maintained by the crown.
In Canada we adopted a slightly different principle. Our standing army has never been large. The militia was permanently enrolled, mainly for the instruction of the non-permanent militia, for running the schools, to man certain forts and to look after warlike stores. We have never had anything in the nature of a standing army, but now it is suggested that there may be a field force, an airborne brigade and a mixed brigade; all very small, but in the nature of a standing army of regular troops.
At the same time, this parliament is being asked to give up its right to protect the people of this country. It is being asked to hand over to the governor in council the sole authority for increasing that force to whatever size the governor in council may desire. That is one of the fundamental principles for which the British people have struggled for centuries. It is one of the principles that we in this parliament cannot surrender.
This bill to amend the Militia Act is simply a series of unimportant amendments which hide and cloak one vital, fundamental principle. I submit that it is unnecessary at this time and we of this party will oppose the
Militia Act

second reading unless the minister is prepared to say that he will establish a limit to the size of the forces which are to be permanently or regularly enrolled and to be known as the active army. That would only be following out what has been the principal practice of Canadian policy for the last fifty or sixty years.
I ask the minister to state definitely in his closing remarks whether he is prepared to amend section 22 so that there will be a definite ceiling. I do not ask him to amend it now; it can be amended when we are in committee. If he gives us the assurance that he will agree to setting a ceiling so that the constitutional practice of government of the military forces by the parliament of this country will be continued, then we can discuss in committee any amendments that we may suggest to the minor clauses. But if he will not give us that assurance now, we are opposed to the passing of the second reading of this bill.
