Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to say anything on this bill until we got into the committee stage, but I should like to make a few observations before the second reading passes. I wish to disagree with the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Jaques), and I hope he will agree that I should disagree with him when he reads the statement of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) a little more carefully than apparently he listened to it. It is not a question of this group waving a red flag. Nobody in this group waves a red flag. But we do recognize that there is in this world a nation over which the red flag flies and which is tremendously powerful. It may be a very good friend and possibly at some time it might be a very powerful enemy of this country. I do not know what history is going to bring. But we are very much concerned to see that our own independent national life in this country is maintained.
I agree with the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) on two counts:	first, that we
should have a Canadian army act. There is no necessity for having any part of our Militia Act subject to the operation of the British army act. I agree with him on another count most heartily, and that is that these amendments would hand over to the government powers which should be in the hands of parliament itself to determine the size of our army.
There is another feature of the bill which I look upon with alarm. I know, Mr. Speaker, that we are not supposed to pick out particular sections of the bill and discuss them on the second reading, but I think it is in order for me to say that, within the amendments proposed, there are possibilities of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) having a very big hand in shaping Canadian foreign policy, in that he is permitted to do certain things which, coupled with the Prime Minister's
statement of yesterday, would give him tremendous powers in the formation of Canadian foreign policy. I do want to see friendship with the United States. I do want to see friendship with every single nation in the world that wants to be friendly with us and to join the united nations and assist that organization in bringing about the peace for which we all hope. I do not want to see Canada at the present time, within that united nations organization or outside it, make military or other alliances or commitments which may in some future year prove to have been wrong.
If some of the things I foresee in this are done-and they can be done-we may find ourselves in the position of having said at this time, without any occasion for it, that, regardless of what happens in the future, we are definitely committed to fight on the side of another nation even though she is wrong. I believe there was once a man who said, "My country, right or wrong." I would like to be always able to say, "my country right." I do not want us to be wrong if we can avoid it.
These things can happen. I remember when I was a young man, young enough to be in the last war, we thought Japan was a grand, courageous, democratic, cultural and progressive country. We almost exhausted the dictionary in our search for superlatives to describe the virtues of the Japanese. Thirty years later, we exhausted the same dictionary for superlatives to describe their iniquities. I can remember not so many years ago when this country and a great many others were very fearful of the role which the Soviet Union was going to play in world war II. I can remember also the victory loan drives of only a few years ago, in which I took an active part, where moving pictures were shown from the national film board and from departments of the United States government, where military commanders were quoted as saying that the great fight of the Russian army had saved civilization. Within a few years, there was a change from a feeling of antagonism to one of intense friendship, and now possibly to one, if not of antagonism, of suspicion and distrust.
This can happen with any nation again. Let me remind the house that conflict between this country and the friendly nation to the south is not unknown in our Canadian history. Conflict between that country and Britain is not unknown in history. I hope it never repeats itself; but it could happen, and if that situation should arise at some time, is Canada to be in the position of having been thrown into a foreign policy, a commitment which at that time, under the conditions that might arise,
Militia Act

would prove to have been very faulty and to have thrown us on the side we definitely would not want to be on?
I see no reason why we cannot be a nation by ourselves, friendly to every other nation that wants to be friendly with us, cooperative in every respect, but completely in charge of our own housekeeping, and if there are cobwebs in our house we shall take them out ourselves and let the other fellow deal with his.
I believe that in these amendments there are opportunities for these considerations to be disregarded and to give us too close a connection which we may sometime regret.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
should like to take up a somewhat strange statement of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion). In rising a moment ago to explain, or perhaps justify his intention to vote with the friends who sit on his right, the hon. member said he could not support this bill because it confirms the principle of compulsory military service in time of peace and gives the governor in council the right to establish conscription in this country.
After a close examination of the bill, for I have had occasion to give it careful study, I must state that no part of it grants such power to the governor in council. The explanatory notes, which are quite clear, state the reasons for its introduction. I note that in his statement, the hon. member was careful not to say what section confirms this principle.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION

I
had no right to say it, but will do so when the opportunity arises.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: The hon. member will have such an opportunity when we take it up in committee, but I cannot help feeling that the hon. member would have acted with more fairness and honesty if he had explained his point instead of making such a gratuitous statement in the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Defence) (Text):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
In the course of this debate, it has been suggested that it would have been more appropriate had I begun the debate with a comprehensive statement on defence policy and on the work that has been done in the department since my appointment two months ago today. My own view was that that introduction as well as the debate that would follow it would be premature in view of the fact that we had not yet before us the estimates of the Department of National Defence, which will be produced by the

Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in a few days' time when he puts his estimates before the house. My thought was that, following their tabling, we could then have a more detailed and orderly discussion on the subject, and I must say with respect that the discussion that we have had makes me believe that that view was correct.
In the discussion, two points were made with regard to matters in the bill to which I should refer at once. In the first place, it was suggested that, in the proposed amendment to section 22 of the Militia Act, the bill was departing from the time-honoured principle that parliament should control the size of the standing army. Reference was made, and quite properly made in that connection to the Bill of Rights from which that constitutional principle, I believe, flows.
Hon. members will appreciate that it was necessary to amend section 22, which limits the size of the full-time permanent force of Canada to 10,000 men, because we have a full-time force of several times that, and we intend to have a full-time active force of several times that. Since it was necessary to make a change, the question was, what figure would be introduced as a ceiling on the size of the armed forces?
It occurred to us that it would be difficult to fix a figure which was neither so high as to be misleading of so low as to be cramping. In this connection, I would call to the attention of hon. members the fact that it has not been the practice in Canada to pass an annual army act, as they do in the United Kingdom, and that therefore it has not been the practice for us to say by legislation what the size of the permanent force will be.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: We have had a ceiling.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
We have had a ceiling but we have not fixed it each year. It also occurred to us, when considering this matter, that it might be necessary, if the international situation deteriorated and there was a real expectation of war, to increase the figure sharply. If that were done, then it would of itself tend to aggravate the bad situation. For that reason, we felt that the best way in which parliament would exercise control over the size of the permanent force was by its control of the money appropriated for the permanent force and, indeed, for all the defence forces of Canada, and that through that means parliament itself has the most effective control of the size of the armed forces of Canada. That was the view which led the government to draft the clause as it is. However, since this is questioned by two parties in the house, and there is no difference in principle, we are

Militia Act
prepared to do it the other way and to put in a ceiling. I will discuss with my colleagues what the ceiling will be, and I hope hon. members will realize that it will be difficult to fix a ceiling that really will be realistic. This ties in with what I said before about our intention to have in Canada an army act of our own. When we have that, I should think we might very well consider following the British practice of having an annual army act, so that the control of parliament would be exercised in exactly the same way as it is exercised there.
Another matter that wTas referred to was that raised with regard to the control by parliament of any force that may be placed on active service. This control is already in existence in the Militia Act. Section 66 reads as follows:
Whenever the Governor General places the militia, or any part thereof, on active service, if parliament is then separated by such adjournment or prorogation as will not expire within ten days, a proclamation shall be issued for the meeting of parliament within fifteen days, and parliament shall accordingly meet and sit upon the day appointed by such proclamation, and shall continue to sit and act in like manner as if it had stood adjourned or prorogued to the same day.
This section gives the most effective control to parliament that can be given.
In the course of the discussion, suggestions were made by some hon. members that the bill gave increases of power to the government or to the minister. I must say that the bill was prepared before I came into the department, but I have examined it carefully since then and cannot find any such increase of power given by any provisions. If there are any, we should like to see them and consider them when we reach them. The intention is not to give increases of power. The intention is, by this bill, to secure a more effective, appropriate and up-to-date statutory foundation for our armed forces.
I should now like to refer to a matter raised by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), in which he asked under what authority the change in the military district from Calgary to Edmonton had been made. He charged, with that great force and vigour to which we are accustomed when he speaks, that there was no statutory authority for this action. The authority is to be found in section 19 of the Militia Act, which is printed in the bill before us. It reads:
19. The governor in council may,
(a)	direct that any portion of Canada shall be a military district for the purposes of this act. and may alter the limits ot any such district;
(b)	cause two or more districts to be grouped together for the purposes of command and administration; and
(c)	divide any military districts into subdistricts, brigade, regimental and company divisions, as appears expedient.
That gives the fullest possible statutory authority for the action which was taken.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: What you have read does not support that, does it?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Yes, it does, completely.
Then the hon. member for Calgary West, with even greater inaccuracy, suggested, indeed charged, that this change in the military district had been made for political purposes. I say that is not so. This change was decided upon before I was in the department, but I have gone thoroughly into it with the officers. I find it was first suggested by the officers of the army for military reasons, and it was based on military grounds exclusively. It was part of a general plan whereby the twelve military districts of Canada were organized into five commands; and those commands were located in centres which took account of the strategic and geographical situation of the country. The commands were located in order that the most effective coordination and cooperation might be secured within a given area with not only the forces of the army but also those of the navy and air force. The location of the five commands had regard to the very considerable developments that have occurred during the war. In the case of Calgary and Edmonton, regard was had particularly to the existence of the Alaska highway, the northwest staging route and the development of the far north. As I say'-and I repeat it-this change was decided upon on the recommendation of the military authorities for strategic, geographical and economic reasons, and for no others.

speechtext: What are they?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) did not hear about, this change until it had been decided upon. I hope that the statement which I have made will put an end to charges for which there is no foundation whatever.
I should like to follow some of the invitations that have been extended to deal with the work of the department and the organization of defence in a general way. A good many statements have been made here today which are based on nothing but imagination, which misrepresent the situation and which, if left uncontradicted, will of themselves do the very thing which some of the speakers predicted, namely, affect the morale of the
Militia Act

forces and also the confidence of the people. It will be those statements that do it and not anything that has happened or is likely to happen in the Department of National Defence.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
It was the minister's silence that was doing it.
Some lion. MEMBERS: Order.

speechtext: The minister's silence was doing it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
In the two months during which I have been in the department I must say I have not made many speeches about atom bombs or guided missiles or jet-propelled planes or other things to make people's flesh creep. I thought it was my job first to do what obviously was wanted, not only by the government but by the people of Canada and by the members of the armed services themselves; that is, to endeavour to coordinate the three departments which had been developed separately during the war. The departments, as hon. members know, each had almost a complete set of civilian services, while the services themselves had three sets of almost everything. That was perhaps natural and proper during the war, but certainly it was not the soundest foundation on which to build good defence forces in peace.
At the end of the war-and I would remind hon. members that the war has been over for only eighteen months-we had an organization and departments which had been dealing with armed services which had increased a hundredfold. First, to be tackled was the work of repatriation, demobilization and rehabilitation. This immense job has proceeded rapidly and smoothly in consequence of the careful planning and fine cooperation by everyone concerned. That was the first thing the defence forces had to deal with at the end of the war, repatriation, demobilization and rehabilitation; and I say to this house and to the country that the job has been magnificently done, and reflects the greatest possible credit on the members of the armed services, on the transportation companies, on the officers of the government and on everyone else who had anything to do with that important work.
But not only was it necessary to demobilize the armed forces, the personnel; there was also a big job to be done in liquidating the materials of war that we had on hand at the end of hostilities. That work also has been pushed ahead. We had hundreds of millions of dollars worth of military equipment on hand in Canada at such places as the Longue
fMr. Claxton.]
Pointe depot, one of the great storehouses of the world, where there are twelve buildings, each 600 feet by 260 feet, with twenty-four miles of railway track, with munitions and materials of war of every kind. All that had to be gone over and prepared for disposal by War Assets Corporation if it was surplus to requirements, or put away to be used for mobilization reserve, or made available to the active and reserve armies. That job also is well advanced.
These two operations have required a very large staff of civilian personnel in the three departments. As the job is being pushed forward, we are able to reduce material!}' the civilian personnel, and we hope to get it down to a proper post-war basis in the course of the next year. But this operation of liquidation and organization will still take more than a year to complete. It is a reflection of the immense war effort of Canada that there should be so much to be done afterwards.
Then in the department itself it was necessary to set under way the job of coordinating the three departments. As a first step, it was decided to locate the department in the three buildings on Cartier square. The move began about four weeks ago and is already well advanced. The whole department and the defence headquarters are being established in the three buildings. The plan is that the minister and deputy minister, chiefs of staff and the policy-making and administrative organization will be in the front building, formerly the old naval building. The supply, equipment and engineering services of the three services will be in what was the army annex, and personnel and similar services will be in the Lisgar building, formerly occupied by the air force. We propose to merge all the civilian services that have been in the three departments and gradually to have the functions of the various branches amalgamated so that the civilian services for the entire Department of National Defence will be done by one group of officials and employees. Similarly it is proposed to consolidate a great many of the auxiliary services of the armed services themselves. This includes the chaplain, medical, dental, hospital, welfare, education, legal and public relations services of the armed forces. The exact way in which that will be done is still being worked out. With regard to matters of supply, transportation and the like, there will be a good deal of consolidation; and with regard to operations, training and planning there wall be close coordination under the direction of the three chiefs of staff who together form a committee.

Militia Act
I should tell the house that, in beginning these plans and in carrying them out, there has been nothing but the most splendid cooperation on the part of the officers of the department, the chiefs of staff and all those who have worked under them. They have carried on their work in difficult circumstances.
While this has been going on, we have had to consider again the post-war defence needs of Canada and what we should do during this year. Hon. members will agree-it is shown in the debate we have just had-that no one can say what the shape of the next war will be, if there is one; and certainly the best thing any of us can do about that is to use our utmost endeavours to prevent another war from ever happening. But it is necessary that we should have in Canada certain forces; and the size and extent of those forces will, of course, depend in part on the geographical situation in this country and its resources, and, above everything else, on what possible threat or danger we might have to meet.
I am in a postiion which, I think, is well understood by hon. members when I say it is difficult for any member of a government, and particularly the Minister of National Defence, to put before either parliament or the people all the considerations which enter into the making of a defence policy. In the very nature of things it is not possible to do that. But I should like to point this out, that if we at once recruited' our three services up to the ceilings that were announced by my predecessor last year, and) fill u.p the establishments on the basis set forth by him, it would be difficult at a later time to make any change which might be desirable in order to meet any changing situation. It seems to me that we are on much safer ground if, for this year, we limit the recruiting of the defence forces of Canada to seventy-five per cent, as I have announced. Then, at the end of the year we would be able to see better what the future holds for us, and how best we can plan expansion' in any direction or other changes which may seem necessary at that time.
The situation with regard to recruiting has been described as unsatisfactory by some hon. members. To the contrary, the navy has recruited to within seventy-five per cent of the ceiling. That is, it is at the figure of about 7,500. That is the permanent force navy. The air force is at about seventy-five per cent.
On this account for the time being we shall only accept recruits for the navy and air force if they have exceptional qualifications, or if required to fill up gaps in the various branches in respect of which there may be some shortages. That is a good position to be in. With regard to the army, recruiting has advanced well, and the active army is about fifty per cent recruited. Recruits are coming in without any campaign, at a rate which would indicate that we are very likely to achieve the seventy-five per cent during the course of the current year. The officers and men who are joining the armed forces are Canadians with good qualifications. They are splendid Canadians. They have good educational qualifications, good professional qualifications and good physical qualifications.
The rates of pay that they receive were put on an equal basis as among the three services last year, and they are paid at a rate which compares most favourably with rates of pay in civilian occupations. The Canadian- armed forces are good, and the men in it receive- food, clothing, and equipment as good as we can find, and in every way suitable for the good men they are. We do not aim to have anything second rate about the armed forces of Canada.
There has been almost an effort made to misrepresent the situation in respect of the reserves. The figure of 180,000 was announced as the establishment for the reserve forces of Canada. Before the war, in what was then known as the non-permanent active militia- it has since become the reserve army

there were approximately 46.000 soldiers. In no year did more than 15,000 attend camp. What we have proposed is that this year eighty per cent of the officers, 100 per cent of the non-commissioned officers and men of about the number there now are in the reserve force should have thirty days' training. Then there are fifteen days additional for tradesmen. That is much more than- was ever given before. No establishment of any reserve unit has been cut. Further, the reserve units are now furnished with full-time administrative and training officers. They are being given the most modern equipment. Adjustments are being made with respect to the contingent payments made to unit commanders to cover the general expenses of their units; and in every reasonable way we are endeavouring to meet the needs in this country of a reserve force.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: What is the present strength?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
It is over 30,000, which -is very fair when one considers that we are just eighteen months beyond the cessation of hostilities.
I mention the reserve army particularly because we realize its importance. Before seeing service overseas during the first world war, I was in a militia unit and also in the reserve after the end of the last war, and I
Militia Act

know something of the difficulties in connection with training and recruiting reserve units which were experienced after that war. I believe that this time we are setting about meeting those difficulties in a constructive way.
A few weeks ago I met the officers of the council of defence associations and discussed the whole situation with them. I promised them to make the statement which was mentioned by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness), urging the people of Canada to support the reserve force.
Means are being provided for a very considerable amount of training, including flying, in connection with auxiliary air squardons. While I do not have in mind the exact number of days of training, it is about sixty days. The divisions of the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve will also be provided for.
With regard to cadets, the change announced is that we will bring the army cadet training into line with that for the navy and air force, and limit the training to the boys who can benefit from it. Those are boys between fourteen and eighteen years of age. On that account, instructions have been issued to stop the training of junior cadets under fourteen at the end of the present school year. The number of cadets provided for is the number of those aged from fourteen to eighteen. So that there will be no change in that respect, except that we shall not provide training for cadets in units of less than twenty.
In the air force and sea cadets, training will be available for those from fourteen to eighteen years of age, and on an even more extensive basis than in the army.
While discussing another matter today, I referred to defence research. All hon. members recognize its importance. Canada made great contributions in the field of research during the war, and it is our aim to continue that work. I believe Canada is the only country which has set up a defence research board with a director general who holds a position equivalent to that of a chief of staff. The director general of defence research is a member of the chiefs of staff committee and also of the defence council.
In addition, we recognize the importance of industrial organization. Hon. members appreciate the fact that of the materials made' by Canada, seventy per cent were used by the armed forces of other nations. Our contribution in the field of industry as well as of agriculture to the fight for freedom was astonishing and has been recognized as such by all other nations. We consider it important that industry should continue to be interested in defence
matters and that there should be cooperation and the closest possible relationship between industry which is capable of being used for defence purposes and the armed services therm selves. Plans are being worked out to continue that cooperation. There should be the very closest and most intimate relationship between the services and research and industry.
This has been a summary account of the general situation. I should like and I am prepared to develop all the different aspects of this matter when the defence estimates come up, if there is not an earlier opportunity. I should like the house to appreciate the fact that the kinds' of consideration which hon. members have had in mind during this debate have been in the minds of the government and of the department and of the services while plans were being laid during this difficult period.
We have had six years of war. During that time Canada enlisted something over a million men in the three armed services and, in addition, a large number of women. They formed a great fighting force and their contribution to the cause for which we were fighting was recognized everywhere as being a great contribution. It was my privilege to be in Paris at the conference on the treaties of peace with the five satellites of Germany and, while there, I had a good many opportunities of seeing the representatives of other countries who were attending that conference. I had a chance to visit the battlefields over which our troops fought during the war. AVe had in the armed forces of Canada the best ambassadors any country could have. They left behind them a reputation for hard fighting, yes, but also for decent conduct second to none. Everywhere I heard expressed admiration, for our armed forces and for the industrial effort of Canada and for the great contribution made by our farmers to meet the needs of Europe.
That was the story one heard everywhere. People expressed respect for what Canada had done in the war and for what she has contributed to the cause of peace since the war. Our view is that we can have in Canada a defence force which will live up to the great reputation made by those who served before them in two world wrars. Our belief is that we can have an effective and efficient defence force which will be of a nature to enable us to say with pride that they are carrying on in. the best Canadian traditions.
I have no need to assure this house that those forces will never be used except in the defence of Canada and Canada's vital interests. We will never enter into any war of aggression, and the suggestions sometimes made by others to that effect can readily be ignored.

Printing of Parliament
The suggestion was made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that we should cooperate with other nations in addition to the United States. Of course we shall be glad to do that; but when there are two nations which have such friendly relationships as the United States and Canada, which have such common interests, it is only common sense to expect them to cooperate together. With regard to showing the representatives of other nations what is going on, as hon. members know there is a testing station at Churchill. Arrangements have been made for the military attaches of other nations and for some members of the press to visit that station. That is desirable so long as we receive reciprocal treatment from the other nations, but it may be difficult to continue this kind of relationship unless treatment is given on a more reciprocal basis.
One further word with regard to the whole question of the north. There is a great deal of rather idle speculation about developments there and I hope the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mackenzie King) history making statement of yesterday will go a long way toward meeting that. There is to be the first public showing of the film "Exercise Musk-Ox" at the Capitol theatre at 3.15 o'clock on Sunday afternoon, and I hope hon. members who are interested in the subject will take advantage of this opportunity to see what was done on that trip when forty-seven Canadians travelled some 3,000 miles through the north. They will then be able to appreciate the nature of the problems involved in northern travel and exploration and they will see some of the civilian advantages that were gained from that trip.

I wonder if the minister will permit one question before he finishes, in view of the statement made by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) that we could not support the measure unless the government was prepared to amend section 9 of the bill? My understanding is that the minister said he would so amend the bill, but in order that there may be no misunderstanding I should like to state my question clearly. Am I correct in my understanding of the minister's statement-
Mr. MacIvINNON: Who wrote it?

speechtext: The Minister of Trade and Commerce will get his in due course.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext: Thank you.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Am I correct in my understanding of the minister's statement that he is now willing so to amend section 9 of the bill in committee as to have fixed by statute
a ceiling on the number of the active forces rather than to leave that figure as is proposed in the bill before us to be fixed by order in council? If the answer is yes, we will support this bill. If the answer is no, we cannot support it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO FACILITATE CANADIAN ARMY REORGANIZATION
speechtext:
The statement I made was to that effect except that I added that parliament will have control. As I suggested before, we will consider whether we should not have in future years an annual army act as they have in Britain.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, this bill does not contain any fundamental changes. It only contains the changes that are necessary to enable us to carry on the affairs of the department, pending the time when we can introduce a fundamental revision of the whole act. On that account, for the reasons I have given, I commend the bill to the favourable consideration of the house.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie the house adjourned at 10.55 p.m.
